input.content:
# Chapter 2 — The Fragment

The window in the fourth-period classroom faced south, over the road and the bluff edge, and from it on a clear day the harbor was visible — the channel, the mooring field, the gray stone run of the breakwater. Marcus stood at the window after the Latin students had gone, the eraser still in his hand, looking down at the water. The channel was open. He had passed the harbormaster's shack on his walk to school that morning and it had looked like any morning; the CHANNEL CLOSED board was gone from its post. He turned back to the board.

He was erasing the conjugation table when someone stopped in the doorway.

A young man. Naval officer's uniform, a lieutenant's bars on the collar, a manila envelope held at his side with the precise care of something he had been told to account for. He was perhaps twenty-five, perhaps twenty-six, and he had the look of someone who found school buildings subtly wrong — the chalk smell, the low ceiling, the small benches arranged in rows, the entire category of it. He looked at Marcus with the expression of an errand.

"Dr. Klein. Lieutenant Graves, Rockland district office. The secretary said I might find you here."

"You have." Marcus set the eraser on the chalk rail. He came around the nearest bench. "What can I do for you?"

Graves produced the envelope. He held it out flat, face up, with that same precise care. "We recovered a fragment of paper from the clothing of the man found on the breakwater last month. There are words on it. In German. We were told you're the German teacher."

"I am," Marcus said. He took the envelope.

---

The flap was sealed with adhesive tape. Marcus worked at the tape carefully with a fingernail and drew the contents out onto his palm.

Three inches by two, roughly. It had once been part of a larger piece — the edges were not cut but dissolved, the paper's fiber failing outward from what had been an original tear, so that the boundary between document and nothing was a gradation rather than a line. The ink had run badly. In most places it had spread through the grain of the paper and been taken by the water altogether, leaving brown shadow rather than black letter, abstraction rather than text. He moved to the window and held the fragment up.

In a few places the writing held. Where the ink had been laid down with more pressure — more attention, or more urgency, something that drove the strokes deeper into the fiber before the water had its chance — the letters had outlasted the damage. In the upper third, the remnant of what might have been the start of a salutation: a curved form that the water had met at the second stroke, leaving the first intact and nothing after it. In the body of the letter, two words he could read without hesitation: *kalt* — cold — and, a space away, *ankommen* — to arrive, to reach a destination. Between them a gap from which several lines of text had been taken entirely, the paper there as blank as if it had never been written on.

Near the top of the fragment, in a position consistent with a heading or address block, written in a slightly more upright hand than the body text — a different register, as if the person writing understood that the name was the thing most necessary to survive — a surname, and an initial.

*…Lutz, J…*

He looked at the name for a moment. Then he turned from the window.

"It is a fragment of a personal letter," he said. "Possibly a short note. The legible words in the body suggest cold and arrival — *kalt* means cold; *ankommen* means to arrive, or to reach one's destination. The heading or address block contains a surname and an initial: Lutz, J. Everything else is unrecoverable. Where the paper's fiber has failed, the text is gone."

Graves wrote this in a small notebook. He was thorough in the unhurried way of someone whose thoroughness was a professional trait rather than a personal one.

"Is there more that might come clear? Better light, more time?"

Marcus considered the paper in his hand. He was holding it by the edges. "No," he said. "What is legible is legible because the ink reached further into the paper. The rest has been taken. There is no better light for a question the material itself cannot answer."

Graves put the notebook away. He looked at the fragment, then at Marcus. He was not a suspicious man; he was a man with an errand, and the errand was nearly finished. "I'd appreciate it if you'd keep it a few days," he said. "Have another look. The county examiner's office is still working the case."

"Of course," Marcus said.

He put the fragment back in the envelope. He put the envelope in his coat pocket. Graves thanked him, left his number with the school secretary, and went; his steps went down the hallway in the ordinary unhurried way and diminished. The room was quiet: chalk dust in the window light, the conjugation table half-erased on the board, the passive forms of *amāre* fading from left to right where he had stopped.

---

He walked home along Prospect Street in the last of the afternoon, past the post office and the church and the maple that had shed most of its leaves. The air was cold and held no wind. The envelope was in his coat pocket. He was aware of it the way one becomes aware of a small thing that has been present long enough to feel native to its location — not heavy, not attended to constantly, but present in the way that a specific weight acquires specificity over the course of a day spent not attending to it.

At the Crow house Lillian had made potato soup. She set it on the table without ceremony, brought the coffeepot, and went back to the stove with the economy of a woman who had long since decided that the space between the stove and the table was where she thought best. Henry was already in his chair. He had come home early, he said, because the furnace register in the second-floor corridor had pulled loose from its fitting — a screw problem, easily addressed — and he had wanted to address it before the end of the day.

"The building superintendent would have sent someone," Marcus said.

Henry said: "The building superintendent would have sent someone on Friday." He did not look up from his bowl.

They ate. The radio in the parlor was on at low volume — the evening news, Italy, a road, the calculated cost of something being taken. Marcus had been a European before he had been a resident alien, and when he heard the Italian cities he conducted, privately, the reckoning that the cities required of him, and then he ate his soup. Lillian came in once to refill the coffeepot. She moved through the room the way she always moved through it, which was to say she moved through it as if she owned it, which she did, and as if she were aware of what was in it, which she was.

Marcus thanked her for the soup when she cleared the plates.

"It's potato soup," she said. "I'll take thanks when it's worth the thanks." But she paused in the doorway with the stack of bowls, and the pause had in it the character of something in the neighborhood of affection, and she went in.

Henry folded his hands around his coffee cup. Outside, the maple stood bare against the last grey light. "Good soup," he said.

"Yes," Marcus said.

He went upstairs. The third step creaked, and the seventh. Below him, after a moment, the sound of the kitchen tap.

---

His room was the front room on the second story: a desk, a lamp, a narrow bed, a shelf of books along the south wall — three Latin grammars, a German dictionary, and a copy of Rilke's *Duino Elegies* in a paperback edition that had been in his bag since London and that he had not opened in nearly two years. The window looked east toward the school. The school was dark now; the light over the entrance burned its small steady amber on the sidewalk below.

He draped his coat over the back of the chair. He stood at the window a moment, looking at the entrance light and the empty sidewalk. Then he sat at the desk and took the envelope from his coat pocket and set it under the lamp.

Under the lamp the fragment looked different from how it had looked by the classroom window. The lamp was warm; its warmth brought the shadows in the paper up more clearly. He spent some time — he did not count the minutes — with the paper tilted at different angles in the light, working at what had been asked of him: more, if there was more. In the salutation there was a curve before the dissolved letters that might be the surviving arc of an *A*, or the bottom of a *D*, or neither of these things. The phrase in the body — *kalt* and then the gap and then *ankommen* — gave up nothing further. The gap held what it held, which was a shadow, which was not a word.

He put the paper flat on the desk. He looked at the name.

*Lutz, J.*

The ink there was steady. The letters held their edges without bleeding into the surrounding fiber. It was written in the hand of someone who had understood, when writing it, that the name was the thing most necessary to get down.

Josef Lutz had been at the camp at Sherbrooke for some months when Marcus arrived. He was Viennese — not in the way Marcus was Viennese, not the university version, the assimilated professional version that had believed for too long in its own acceptability and had been made to understand this error in specific terms — but from a different district, a different formation, a different set of available strategies for surviving the discovery that one's acceptability had been provisional. He was a few years younger than Marcus — thirty-nine or forty or forty-one; he was the sort of man who did not offer his age, not from vanity but from the habit of withholding the details that made you locatable. He spoke four languages and said he had a fifth poorly, and Marcus had never learned which fifth it was.

He was quiet. His quietness was not timidity but economy — he spoke when speech served a purpose and was still otherwise, and he had the habit of always knowing where the doors were. Not nervously. He watched them with the settled attention of a man for whom the character of doors — which way they swung, whether they latched, how loud they were, how often they opened and which kinds of people used them — had, at some point, been information worth having.

He had no valid Canadian papers after the camp, which was in some respects why he had been in the camp. He had a cousin in New York, a distant cousin who had gone there in the twenties and was, presumably, still there. Josef was trying to get to him. He said this as a man states a next step that has been interrupted by circumstances he did not generate and does not consider to have permanent authority over his plans. He was trying to get there.

Marcus had been released in the late summer of 1942, by the intervention of a Quaker relief organization that had found him a position at the high school through channels he had never been able to reconstruct to his satisfaction, and he had arrived in Coldwater Reach in September. He had not seen Josef after his own release. He had heard, in the uncertain way of displaced persons whose networks depend on letters that do not always arrive and on people who are not always where they were last heard from, that Josef had been released in late 1942. Or perhaps early 1943; the date did not hold its shape when Marcus tried to fix it.

In the time since, Marcus had told himself that Josef had made it to New York. This was not knowledge. It was a practice — the same practice he had adopted for a number of people from the camp whose subsequent fates were not available to him, the assignment of the better outcome, because the worse outcome required a kind of reckoning he did not have room for. He had been, on the whole, disciplined about it. He had not thought about Josef Lutz since April, and when he had thought about him then it was briefly, and the conclusion had been the same: the cousin, the apartment, the matter resolved. He had thought about him the way one thinks about a closed question.

He looked at the name on the paper.

---

Graves had left his number with the school secretary. In the morning Marcus could find it without difficulty. He could call and report that a further examination had yielded nothing beyond what he had said in the classroom, which was close to accurate: the paper had not given him more than he had translated on his feet. He could return the envelope. He could remain the German teacher, the useful man, the one you brought your translation problems to — occupying the precise amount of usefulness that was required and no further amount.

The difficulty was categorical. He could report nothing further only if what he now held was nothing further, and what he held was a name he knew. A name he knew was not nothing. He had spent the day in the category of useful-and-no-more, and the category had been available to him, and he had occupied it with what he judged was reasonable competence, and it was now past nine in the evening and the category had closed.

He pulled the envelope toward him. He folded down the flap, tucked the fragment inside, and creased it shut.

He opened the bottom drawer of the desk. He set the envelope face-down at the back of it, under the edge of a manila folder. He closed the drawer.

He sat for some time with the lamp on. Through the window the school's entrance light made its small circle on the empty sidewalk. He had known Josef Lutz, who watched doors, who had a cousin in New York, who had been — by Marcus's careful, disciplined, two-year accounting of the matter — all right.

He reached up and turned the lamp out.

The entrance light glowed amber through the glass. Below the floor the house was still.

He did not open the drawer.

input.content:
# Chapter 3 — Allgäu

The second pail was the heavier one.

By the time she set the first down by the side door and went back for it, the cold had committed itself — November pulling warmth out of the barn through the gaps in the board-and-bat siding, through the places where the insulation had thinned over the years and the wind had found its way to the bedding straw. The animals gave heat but not enough; by the second pail Hannah could feel the cold in her fingers and in the tops of her arms, where the muscles went into the shoulder. She had been up since five. The barn smelled of what it always smelled of — manure and hay and the particular sourness of cold milk — and when she had come out of the house in the dark she had heard through the kitchen window the radio already on, Marta up early, listening to the weather news with the careful attention she gave it every morning now.

The truck came at seven. She was still in the middle of the milking and heard the engine from the upper barn, then the silence when it cut, then the sounds of men climbing down from the truck bed. She did not stop. The morning milking was hers regardless; the barn animals did not know anything about trucks.

By the time she finished and carried the first pail out, the crew was dispersed to their work. Two of them were at the far fence line — PW armbands pale against their jackets — and she couldn't make out faces at that distance. She had learned to place them by other signs: by build, by where they were assigned, by the way they moved when Oakes was watching versus when he wasn't. The man at the corner post was Brauer, wide across the back, who never spoke to anyone if he could help it. The other she knew less well; he had been put on fence duty since October and had stayed there. Carvell Oakes was near the south wall examining the water pump housing with deliberate slowness. The cold had been getting into his knees since early in the month, and he moved now with the careful economy of a man rationing his joints. The rifle hung across his back with the strap gone slack on one side.

Werner was in the upper field. She had watched him go up before the truck came, collar turned, moving without hurrying. It was a new habit — being elsewhere when the crew arrived, staying up there until they were gone. She had not asked him about it.

She went back for the second pail.

---

She was setting it down inside the barn corridor when she heard the German.

It was not close — from the far end of the corridor, where the stanchion repairs had been waiting since August. She heard a voice first, then heard it was German. And then — not through the words themselves, but through sound alone, through the thing recognition does before the mind arrives — she heard what kind.

Not the German of the radio. Not the newsreel sound, the shouting sound, the specific German that people now heard in their heads when they heard the word at all. Not the flat classroom German of her eighth-grade workbook before Mr. Parkins retired and they dropped the subject. This was the German her father's kitchen made on a Sunday evening when the radio was off and the week had been hard and Werner stopped, for a little while, being someone who had come to Maine in 1922. Something that happened to the vowels at the back of the mouth — a roundness, a giving-way. The *ch* sounds that arrived instead of scraping. The particular way the end of a word kept its weight.

She hadn't heard that from outside the house in years.

The man speaking was Karl. She knew his build by now, the way you learn a person who works in your field of vision five days a week — not by looking directly, but by the shape they make in the day. He was at the stanchion end of the corridor with Brauer. He said something, holding a length of wire in both hands; Brauer shook his head; Karl said it again, slightly differently. Brauer looked at the wire. Neither of them was looking at her.

She said a word. Just one — *Gell?* — before she thought. The Allgäu particle, the tag that meant *isn't it* or *right?* or sometimes only the breath between sentences, the sound that meant *you see what I mean.* It came out in her father's vowels, her father's consonants, and she heard herself say it and could not put it back.

Karl turned.

His expression was not alarm. It was something she needed a moment to name — a recalibration, the look of a person adjusting you from one category to another. Brauer looked at the south wall of the barn. Outside, Oakes had not moved from the pump housing.

"You speak it," Karl said, in the same dialect.

Not quite a question.

She said: "My father does." Then, because German came easier for it: *Meine Eltern kamen 1922.*

She watched him take that in — the idea of a person from that sound, from those vowels, appearing in a barn in Maine with milk on her apron.

"From near Marktoberdorf," he said. "Karl Reinmar."

She gave her name. He would have heard it already; names move through a farm yard. But saying it directly was different. "My family is from near Kempten."

*Etwa fünfzig Kilometer*, he said. About fifty kilometers.

"Yes," she said.

Oakes was still at the pump housing, weight on his right hip, his back to the barn entrance. She had learned his patterns through October: he made his circuit roughly every twenty to twenty-five minutes, the same route each time, the pace adjusted for the weather and the day's degree of discomfort. She had maybe ten minutes left in this window, maybe less.

*Sind Ihre Eltern noch hier?* Karl asked. Are your parents still here?

She heard the weight in it. *Noch* — still. Not a simple word in 1943.

*Mein Vater ist immer noch von dort*, she said. My father is still from there. She paused. *Das versteht man.* One understands this.

She didn't explain further and he didn't ask her to. He held the wire in both hands without fidgeting. He was nineteen — they had been given the crew's names and approximate ages when the arrangement started, the same way you were given the specifications of new equipment — and he had the quiet of someone young who had already learned that most quiet was safer than most speaking.

He said he was conscripted at eighteen, and he said it in the way you state a thing that no longer requires feeling to state: it happened; the army was assigned to him; he had not chosen it. He had been thinking of a trade before that, he said — a trade, not the army — but then a letter came and the plan became something that had been. Now he was here. No complaint in any of it. The absence of complaint had its own weight, the weight of a person who had done the accounting and come out the other side of it.

Then, as a different thing — in the way you mention a strange bird seen from a moving window — he said he had seen something odd. On the transport from Bangor, in October. The truck driving the coastal road at night, rain coming hard, the windows fogged over. He had cleared a circle on the glass with his sleeve.

An older man on the verge of the road. In the rain, at that hour. Moving at a pace that was — he paused for the word — purposeful, he said. Light on his feet. Carrying something under his arm, or over his shoulder; he could not be certain at that distance, through the rain on the glass. *Ein älterer Mann. Leicht auf den Füßen. Er trug etwas.* Moving in the direction of the water, as best Karl could judge from the moving truck.

*Er schien einen langen Weg vor sich zu haben*, Karl said. He seemed to have a long way ahead of him.

He said it the way you say such a thing: here is what I saw, I do not know what it means, it has stayed with me the way small odd things stay. Hannah listened. Something in her attention had caught — a hook without visible anchor — and then she heard Oakes begin to move on the gravel outside, his uneven footfall coming around the south corner of the barn.

---

Karl's hand came out of his coat pocket. A piece of paper, folded four times — small, barely larger than a matchbook. He pressed it into her palm as she lifted the second pail from the floor. One gesture, quick and deliberate, the way you execute a movement you have rehearsed many times in your mind and are now finally completing in the body.

"Don't read it here," he said. In English, very quiet. Very precise.

He turned back to the stanchion. Brauer had not moved from the wall.

Hannah walked out of the barn with the pail. Oakes was coming around the corner in his hip-careful way. He looked at her and said it was a cold one today. She said it was. She kept walking.

In the dairy she rinsed the pail and hung it. She reached into her apron pocket; the note was there. She moved her fingers away from it. She reached instead for the next hook.

---

She carried it through the afternoon.

Werner came down from the upper field before noon and worked on the harness that had needed restitching for two weeks. The crew was in the yard at intervals. Marta called her in to help with the midday meal and she set the table and heated the bread and ate her own portion standing at the counter. She washed the dishes. She went back out. The note was in her apron pocket through all of it — while her hands were in the feed buckets and the water troughs, while she was walking the fence line to count the boards the wind had loosened — and she did not touch it. She could feel it when she moved: the four folds of it, almost nothing in weight, present the way a small thing becomes present when you are not attending to it.

At half past four the truck came back into the yard for the crew. She was in the dairy and she heard it — engine, the creak of the gate, boots on gravel. She stayed where she was until the truck turned out onto the road. She listened to it going down the gravel until the sound went under the wind.

She went upstairs to change her apron. Werner's boots were on the back step; Marta's voice came from the kitchen. She moved the note from her apron to the pocket of her everyday dress and came back downstairs and helped with the evening milking, and the animals did not know anything about notes.

---

After supper Werner settled at the radio. Marta brought the dish water up. The evening news came steady and measured — Italy, the Pacific, convoys, a reporter's voice from somewhere very far away making the cost of things sound orderly. Werner turned the volume up, then adjusted it down a little, looking for the setting between unendurable and inaudible. Hannah said she was going up.

Her room had the small lamp on the table by the window. She sat on the edge of the bed and took the note from her dress pocket. She held it in both hands a moment — its folded density, the four creases — and then she unfolded it.

The paper was ruled, from a workbook or something like it; the kind of paper that you used carefully because you had counted out what you needed before you wrote. The writing was in pencil, very small and deliberate, each letter formed as by someone for whom writing paper was not a thing to waste.

*Karl Reinmar. Marktoberdorf, Allgäu.*

*Man hat mich eingezogen, als ich achtzehn war — ich wollte Schreiner werden, das war mein Plan. Dann kam ein Brief. Nun bin ich hier.*

*Die Rinder erinnern mich an daheim. Das ist keine Klage.*

*Den Mann auf dem Weg habe ich noch in Erinnerung. Er schien einen langen Weg vor sich zu haben.*

She tilted the paper toward the lamplight. She read it through. Then she read it from the beginning again.

*Schreiner* — her father used the word sometimes, speaking about other men's work. Carpenter. Karl had wanted to be a carpenter. A letter came. She set those three sentences alongside every other account she had heard in four years of a plan interrupted, a letter arriving, a person ending up somewhere else, and they fit without revision, in exactly the proportion he had given them. Three sentences. Not a complaint. This is what happened; now I am here.

*Die Rinder erinnern mich an daheim.* The cattle remind me of home. *Das ist keine Klage.* That is not a complaint.

She looked at the last two sentences longer.

*Den Mann auf dem Weg habe ich noch in Erinnerung.*

The man on the road I still remember.

Below the floor the radio shifted — music now, a woman's voice over something slow and stringed — and Werner's chair moved, and the house settled into its evening sounds.

Hannah folded the note along its four creases and held it in both hands in her lap, under the lamp.

Hannah carries milk pails in the cold barn while the POW crew disperses to farm work; Werner is deliberately in the upper field; Marta is at the kitchen radio. Karl is working in the barn corridor with Brauer when Hannah hears him speak in the Allgäu dialect — the German of her father's kitchen — and says one word (*Gell?*) before she can stop herself. They exchange names and geography in low Allgäu German: she is from near Kempten, he from near Marktoberdorf — about fifty kilometers. Karl mentions his conscription at eighteen (he had wanted to be a carpenter), then, as a small observed thing, describes seeing an older man on the coastal road in the rain in October — light on his feet, carrying something, moving toward the water. Hannah files the detail without knowing what it points toward. When Oakes begins to circle back, Karl presses a small folded note into her palm — 'Don't read it here' in careful English — and turns away. Hannah carries the note all afternoon without opening it. That evening in her room under the lamp she reads it: Karl's name, town, three sentences of conscription story (including his plan to be a Schreiner), a line about the cattle reminding him of home (not a complaint), and the final two sentences about the man on the road. She reads it twice, folds it along its creases, and holds it in both hands. The chapter ends on that image.

input.content:
# Chapter 4 — The Commander

The coffee was the real kind. She had kept the tin at the back of the shelf since Saturday, when she'd walked up to Atwood's and set it aside — a rationed indulgence held back for a use that could justify it. She measured out what was needed and no more. She put the chairs right: her chair behind the desk, the second chair pulled to the side of the desk rather than across it, which was the arrangement she used when she did not want the desk between her and the person she was meeting. She set the log on the stand. She straightened the tide chart where the lower tack had let it slip two inches to the right. She checked the oil burner. She had run out of things to adjust, so she stood at the window and watched the harbor.

The November light came off the water flat and cold. No wind yet, but the sky had the color of something deciding. The channel marker off the south shoulder cycled steady red in the grey. A cormorant worked the near shallows. The two boats still on their moorings this late in the season rode easy.

The Commander's car came down the access road at ten past nine.

---

Commander Horace Willard, Naval District, Rockland. She had spoken with his office by radio on the morning of October 3 and once more in mid-October when the county examiner's report was logged at the district level; she had not met him in person. He was perhaps sixty. The naval overcoat had been broken in correctly — it had lost its stiffness without losing its order. He was a man who had done this kind of work before the war started and would do it after.

He shook her hand at the door.

"Harbormaster Bowman."

"Commander." She stepped back. "I have coffee."

He came in and took the offered chair. She poured two cups and sat down. He placed a small stiff-covered notebook on the desk, opened to a blank page, and set his pen on it. He looked at her once in a level, professional way — the look of someone confirming a match — and then looked at the notebook.

"The third of October," he said. "Start where you started."

---

She started where she'd started. Three-day gale, northeast, wind building from Saturday. Channel closed Monday morning at 1030, conditions deteriorating, navigable water compromised. The walk on October 3: the harbor side first, then the seaward face. The finding at roughly two hundred feet from the pier head. Male, estimated fifty to sixty, no papers on the body, no identification of any kind. Clothing: wool overcoat, wool trousers, leather shoes. Not fishing dress. Not working coast. No oilskin.

She had called the District Commander's office by radio immediately upon returning to the shack and had read them the log entry as written. She had contacted Constable Tibbetts for the local side. The county examiner arrived at half past one with two men and a canvas stretcher. They removed the body, filed a probable-drowning report, divided the form in two and gave her the copy.

The Commander wrote in his notebook without hurrying. When she finished he read back the particulars — dates, times, the chain of contact — and she confirmed them in order.

"The log," he said.

She opened it and put it on the desk in front of him. He read the October 3 body entry once through. He turned back to October 2 and read through the day's entries from the beginning: the morning tide check, the channel closure at 1030, the midday conditions update, the gale report at 1630. At the foot of the October 2 column, below the 1630 entry, he read the 2300 line.

*Weather: NE gale, 35 knots decreasing at first light. Channel: temporarily impaired.*

He read it. He turned ahead to the October 4 and 5 entries. He turned back. He wrote two items from the October 3 entry in his notebook: the distance, two hundred and ten feet, and the phrase *clothing not consistent with fishing or working-coast dress.* He set his pen down.

---

From the inside of his coat he took a manila envelope, opened the clasp, and laid a photograph on the desk.

"Take your time with this," he said.

It was the county photographer's image. She had not seen it before now. The body lay on its side against the seaward face of the breakwater, the granite wet, the overcoat spread around it as the water had arranged it. The man's face was turned slightly toward the camera, the left cheek and jaw and the brow line visible.

She looked at the photograph. She did not reach for it; she looked at it where it lay.

The face of the man in the photograph was the face of someone who had been dead for several days and in the water before that. The features were altered in the way death and water alter things — swollen in places, slack in others, the texture of the skin changed in ways the camera had caught and not softened. She had seen drowned men before. She looked at the cheek, the brow, the set of the jaw. She was looking for what she could say honestly, so she looked with care.

She looked another moment.

She did not recognize him.

"No," she said. "I don't know him."

The Commander returned the photograph to the envelope and closed the clasp.

---

"Any vessel traffic the night before? Night of the second?"

"Gale conditions all through the second," Eira said. "Channel was flagged. No vessel traffic."

He wrote something in his notebook. He looked at the open log where it lay on the desk, ran a finger down the October 2 column without touching the page, and then closed it and handed it across the desk to her.

"Your entries are thorough, Harbormaster."

"That's the requirement," she said.

"It is." He took the notebook in his hand. "Here's where we stand."

---

His office had run the physical description against merchant marine rosters, Allied and German both. Against naval registry, American and German. Against civilian missing-persons reports filed in the four preceding months, coast of Maine and eastern Canada. No match on any of the registries. No match on the missing-persons reports.

"The man will be interred in your town cemetery," he said. "Lacking an identity, that's what we can do for him. The stone will read Unknown Man, October 1943." He looked at her directly. "If anyone comes forward — a letter, a missing report, any information at all — you contact Rockland immediately."

"I will."

"You're the eyes on this harbor, Harbormaster Bowman. You see something that connects, anything at all, you call us."

"Yes," she said.

He closed the notebook. He put his coat on.

---

She walked him out. They went out into the cold. The wind had come up a little from the west. She stood at the shack door and watched him go down the access road to his car. He reversed at the end and turned around and drove out along the road and up the grade toward the main road and was gone.

She went back inside.

---

The shack held its warmth. She moved the coffee cups to the shelf. She put the second chair back to where it belonged. She picked up the log and held it a moment before setting it on the stand.

Then she opened it.

October 2. The morning entries in their order, the channel closure, the afternoon gale report running to 1630. At the foot of the column, in the gap between 1630 and 2300, nothing. Then, at 2300, the weather line:

*Weather: NE gale, 35 knots decreasing at first light. Channel: temporarily impaired.*

Commander Willard had read this line and turned the page. He had not paused at the gap between 1630 and 2300. The log gave him no reason to.

The case was closed. Unknown Man, October 1943.

She put her thumb on the 2300 line. The letters showed at the edges, the rest covered. She held her thumb there.

Then she closed the log.

input.summary: Tuesday, mid-November 1943. Commander Horace Willard of Naval District Rockland visits the harbormaster's shack to take Eira's formal report on the October 3 body finding. Eira prepares with care — real coffee, chairs arranged correctly — and gives her account precisely. Willard asks the close question ("Any vessel traffic the night before? Night of the second?"); Eira says: "Gale conditions all through the second. Channel was flagged. No vessel traffic." She logged none. He accepts this and moves on. Willard delivers the official disposition: no match on merchant marine rosters, naval registries, or missing-persons reports; the man will be interred in the Coldwater Reach town cemetery as "Unknown Man, October 1943"; the case is closed unless new information comes in. Eira is told to contact Rockland if anything surfaces. He leaves. Eira opens the log and puts her thumb on the 2300 line. She closes the log.

# Chapter 5 — The Name

The house had been empty since before eight.

Henry had taken his coat from the hook and gone to the school. A window in the boiler room had lost its latch, he said — the superintendent had been after him about it since October. Lillian had her Ladies' Auxiliary meeting, or possibly the post office; she had been out the door before Marcus finished his coffee. He came upstairs and sat at the desk and looked at the stack of student exercises to his right.

He had not touched them.

The light through the east window was thin and early. The birch stand on the far corner of the school's lot threw long shadows across the frozen ground, and he watched the shadows shorten for something close to twenty minutes without arriving at a decision. The furnace cycled below. The radiator made its knock. No human sound from below, or adjacent. This was the silence of an unoccupied house — different from the silence of his room when Henry and Lillian were below; different again from the silence of the school on a cold morning. This was the particular silence of a house where no one was waiting for anything of him, which was the silence in which a person ran out of reasons to hold off.

He opened the bottom drawer.

---

The magnifying glass had been in his left coat pocket since Vienna. He took it out as he lifted the manila folder away from the fragment — the glass small, German-made, the brass casing worn smooth along the top and left side where his thumb rested. A scholar's instrument: bought secondhand at the University quarter, carried through every subsequent address. He set it beside the lamp.

He turned the fragment face-up.

He had looked at it before. Three evenings since Graves left, perhaps four. He understood the difference between looking and working. He had been looking: the lamp at the wrong angle, the glass out but not properly held, some reason each time to put it back. He adjusted the lamp now so the light fell across the surface at an oblique angle rather than directly down. At direct angle the dissolved ink disappeared into the fiber. Oblique brought the surface into relief — the impressed marks where the nib had pressed fiber down, the shadow of what was there even where the ink had gone.

He held the glass over the heading block.

*Lutz, J.*

The letters were block-formed — a more deliberate hand than the body text, the kind of lettering a person used when they needed a name to remain legible above everything else. *L-u-t-z,* comma, space, *J,* period. He had known this the evening Graves set the envelope on his desk. The glass confirmed it; the letterforms were complete, each one unambiguous.

He moved to the body text.

*Kalt.* Cold. One word, context dissolved on all sides. *Ankommen* — to arrive; the prefix compound was clear, and the fiber below the *k* showed the density of a double consonant. He had given Graves these two words. It was as far as he had permitted himself to go.

The oblique angle changed what was available.

A date block appeared in the upper right quadrant — he had seen its shape before without recognizing it for what it was. *Okto—*, the rest consumed in the damage to the page's lower quarter. October. The year's last digit was gone, and the three before it; the range was 1940 to 1945 and he could not narrow it further.

To the left of the date: a name fragment. The first two letters clear, the rest dissolved to fiber. *Qu—.* Upper case, a proper noun. He brought the glass closer. The letterforms were not ambiguous: *Q* and *u*, and then the fiber had failed. He did not let himself treat the obvious reading as the only reading, but he did not exclude it. *Qu.* Quebec, if the obvious reading held.

Near the bottom left corner, the fragment he had seen before but not trusted — the ink there damaged differently, smeared rather than dissolved, dragged across the fiber before it had dried:

*...nicht mehr warten...*

*Warten:* to wait. *Nicht mehr:* no longer. The surrounding sentence was gone; what remained was the idiom and the state it named. *Can wait no longer.* Or: *no longer able to wait.* Both readings came out in the same place.

He set the glass down.

The case Marcus had declined to construct for ten days could be constructed as follows. A German-language note recovered from the body of an unidentified man found on a Maine breakwater in October of some year. A name, *Lutz, J.*, written in block letters above text mentioning cold and arrival. A proper noun whose first two letters suggested Quebec. A phrase about the end of waiting. The man Josef Lutz, whom Marcus had known at the Sherbrooke internment camp in Quebec, was Viennese, Jewish, trained as an archivist, and had been released from the camp sometime in late 1942 or early 1943, under papers too limited to be safe, with a destination in New York that was accessible from the Maine coast by routes a man without proper papers might reasonably take.

This was the argument from available elements. It was not a proof. Marcus was not in the business of proofs.

---

Josef Lutz had been in the bunk two rows from Marcus's in the B-block at Sherbrooke. Between them in that direction: forty men. In the other direction: twelve. Marcus knew these numbers because in the early months he had counted — the bodies between himself and each door, each exit, each possible approach. Josef Lutz had done the same thing. Marcus recognized it without acknowledging the recognition, because acknowledging it would have required naming what both of them were doing, and there were things you did not name in the camp.

Josef watched doors. When a door opened his attention moved to it first — before the face of whoever was behind it, before the content of whatever was being announced. Which way the door swung. Whether it opened from inside or outside. How quickly and how far. It was not a nervous habit. It was an attentive one. The distinction was not small.

They spoke carefully, as everyone spoke carefully, in the language that sorted you into categories. Josef's German was Vienna German — the university and the archive, the phrasing Marcus recognized from before. He had been training as an archivist. He knew the building on Josefsgasse, the card catalog organized by provenance rather than subject, the particular smell of the basement stacks where the leather bindings had softened in the damp. He described these things with the close, specific attention of a man who could see them clearly because they were not in front of him anymore.

He spoke four languages fluently and a fifth poorly; he mentioned the fifth without identifying it, and Marcus did not ask, because you did not ask questions that invited reciprocal questions about things you also preferred not to name.

When Marcus left — the Quaker placement had come through, the late-summer transport was waiting — he shook Josef's hand at the gate. He remembered the hand. The grip brief and calibrated, exactly the kind of handshake that communicated nothing, which was therefore communicating everything it had available. Josef said something. The gate was making noise; the transport truck was running. Marcus did not hear it clearly. He nodded. He got into the truck.

He had told himself, because a person has to tell themselves something, that Josef had reached New York. That the cousin in the garment trade had been found. That the arrangement had worked, in the way arrangements sometimes did. He had told himself this for fourteen months, with the consistency of a man who understood that the alternative was not something he had room for in the accounting he was running.

He looked at the fragment.

*Nicht mehr warten.* October. *Qu—*. A long way from New York. Not the route Marcus would have chosen; but Marcus had not been the one doing the choosing.

---

He took a sheet of paper from the center drawer. He wrote the address from memory — Simon Ehrlich, at the house in Côte-des-Neiges; he kept the address in his head, where it was available when needed and not available to anyone else. Ehrlich had been at Sherbrooke for eight months, released through a sorting that Ehrlich had the sense not to contest. He had moved to Montreal and set up a clearinghouse for refugee inquiries, operating under cover of a book distribution concern. Marcus had not written to him in fourteen months.

He wrote three paragraphs. He wrote them as a man writes when the only reader he is imagining is the one he intends: directly, the names named, the question stated. He wrote Josef's name twice, the surname once. He wrote the word *Maine* in the third paragraph and stopped and read back what he had.

He read it the way a censor would — not for meaning but for configuration, for the shape that the elements made together. A German-speaking man, formerly in a Quebec internment camp, at a Maine coast address, writing to a refugee clearinghouse in Montreal, asking about a missing German Jew. The censor would not have his particular context. The censor would not need it.

He carried the sheet downstairs to the kitchen.

The stove still had coals from the morning. He opened the front gate and put the paper in. The edges caught first, curling before they took; then the face went brown and then black, the words going last at the center where the fiber was thickest. He watched it until it was finished. He was not disturbed by this. He had burned letters before, in other cities, for other reasons, and the practice was the same each time: you waited until it was done, and then you closed the gate. He closed the gate and went back upstairs.

---

The second letter required a different architecture.

He began with the school, because the school was the ground on which he was permitted to stand without explanation. His advanced German students had exhausted the school's existing materials; he was writing to ask whether Ehrlich's distribution network might have access to German-language graded readers or grammatical workbooks suitable for secondary classroom use; were there channels through which such texts might become available? This was a genuine problem — he had been meaning to address it since September. He added a sentence about the school's coal situation and the dependability of the furnace. This occupied another line.

In the second paragraph: he found himself thinking often of people from the Sherbrooke period; he hoped Ehrlich and his family were well; he wondered, as an aside, whether Ehrlich had heard anything of Josef Lutz — he believed Josef had intended to go to New York after his release, to a cousin there, but he had lost touch entirely and would be glad of any news, if Ehrlich happened to have it.

He read this version twice. Then a third time, from the beginning, more slowly.

The academic paragraph was true and therefore stable. The personal inquiry was dressed as the kind of inquiry old acquaintances made when they had lost track of mutual friends. There was nothing in the letter that named the harbor. Nothing that named the month or any circumstance that connected his Maine address to anything besides teaching and cold weather.

It was possible. Not safe; he did not believe in safe. But possible.

He folded the letter once and put it in the bottom drawer, next to the fragment. He did not address an envelope. He did not take his coat from the hook or count his ration of coins for the post-office window.

He sat at the desk for a moment. Then he pulled the student exercises in front of him and uncapped the red pen.

---

Henry came back in the early afternoon smelling of coal dust, the boiler-room window latched now, and mentioned that the superintendent's approach to window problems in that building was to nail the affected window shut and open a different one — workable, Henry allowed, if you didn't need the original window, which apparently nobody had in three years. Lillian came in from her errand with sugar and a view on the current rationing situation at Atwood's that she held until dinner. Marcus drank his tea and helped carry the packages from the entry.

At dinner they had bean soup from the pot Lillian had started before she left, and bread, and butter. Henry had a letter from his nephew — the young man was in the Pacific, in good health, and had written a passage about the Navy's approach to food that Henry read aloud once and then read again because it was worth hearing twice. They were quiet a moment after the second reading. Marcus ate his bread.

He washed the cups after and dried them and put them on the shelf and came upstairs.

He sat at the desk and brought the lamp to its reading angle and opened the first exercise. He had started it before supper; the case error was marked, the note written in the margin. He turned to the second. The student was working through the third conjugation with more confidence than accuracy; Marcus marked four instances and wrote two corrections, brief and specific, and moved to the third exercise. He worked through to the end of it. His marks were small and took up little room on the page.

He put the cap on the pen.

Outside the window, the November dark had settled over the school and the birch stand and the frozen road. The furnace knocked once below and was still. The drawer was in the desk, and the desk was in the lamplight, and the house was quiet around him.

input.content:
# Chapter 6 — The Lining

The ice had come in the night. Thin, pale at the edges of the drainage channels where the water moved slowest, and the fields beyond had a grey shine to them that meant the ground had given up whatever warmth it had been holding. Hannah carried the first bucket from the pump house to the barn and her breath came out white and the mud at the barn door had gone hard as fired clay underfoot.

In the yard Werner was already out, his work coat buttoned to the collar, one hand on the wire at the far fence post. He hadn't started on the fence.

The truck was late.

It came up the road at nearly eight-thirty — she could hear the engine a quarter-mile off, coming through the tree line before the headlights showed. Werner turned when he heard it but didn't come in from the fence. Hannah set the bucket just inside the barn door and waited.

The truck stopped in the yard and the men got down — Karl first, then Brauer, then the two others. Oakes climbed down last from the cab, rifle strap gone slack on one side, and said something to the driver; the truck backed up and turned and went back out the way it came. Karl had already lifted a coil of fencing wire from the truck bed and was carrying it toward the lower field. He moved the same way he always moved, deliberate and even, his breath clouding against the cold air.

Werner watched him the whole way.

She was looking at her father's back, at the set of his shoulders, the hand still resting on the wire. His face was turned toward Karl. He was not examining the fence post; she had understood this from the moment she came out into the yard, before she was ready to understand it. What she read in the set of him was not anger. Not the careful blankness of a man performing unconcern. Something that cost more than either of those things — a quality of recognition and what the recognition required of him, visible in his back before she could name it in his face, which she could not see.

She went inside with the bucket.

---

The morning moved. Hannah worked the barn interior — the feed, the stall cleaning, the second watering, a gutter to clear that she had been meaning to get to for a week. Werner came through twice: once to find a post maul, once to say something about the south fence needing another post before the ground froze solid. He did not explain the fence post by the road. She did not ask.

She could hear Brauer and Karl on the fence line, intermittent — the sound of the wire stretcher, the knock of a post hammer in cold air. Oakes moved through the yard once, his slow careful steps, and went to the wagon shed and didn't come back. Hannah kept to the barn interior. The cattle were restless by mid-morning, the wind coming from the northwest, and she worked through their agitation without hurrying. Outside, the frost had not melted. The drainage channels held their skim of ice all morning.

She thought, *drei Wochen*, and caught herself. Three weeks she had had the note — had transferred it from dress pocket to coat pocket every morning and back every evening, a practice she had settled into so gradually that she hadn't noticed it becoming a practice until now, counting in German.

She put the thought down and cleared the gutter.

Brauer came to the barn door late in the morning with a question about the wire stretcher's left jaw. She answered him in English without looking up from what she was doing, and he thanked her and went back. She didn't know whether Karl was close enough to hear. The wind was up.

---

The truck came back at three.

She heard it at the gate and went to stand in the barn door. The men lined up without ceremony — the practiced sorting of people who have done this many times — and Oakes walked them over. Karl set something in the truck bed before he climbed up, and she couldn't see what, a coil of wire maybe, and he moved without pausing. The truck turned in the yard.

He did not look toward the farmhouse window as it went.

The not-looking. It was not the same as looking away.

She stayed in the barn door until the truck sound had gone back through the tree line and there was nothing left of the afternoon but low December light coming flat over the east fields, and then she went in to finish the work.

---

In the farmhouse it was warm and already dark outside by five. Marta had the kitchen lamp on and the table half-set — the American flag placemats laid at each place, the ones with the small gold eagle in the corner that she had ordered from Atwood's last spring after reading something in the newspaper. Marta set them out every evening now with a care Hannah recognized as effort, a thing requiring daily renewal. Hannah did not say anything about the placemats. She took off her coat and hung it on the hook behind the door.

She put her hand into the right pocket.

The note was there, folded in its four folds, the paper cool against her fingers. She had moved it from the dress pocket this morning the same as every morning — three weeks, the same motion, until the motion no longer felt like a decision. She held it a moment through the wool.

Werner was at the radio, his chair pulled close. The evening news was on — she could hear it from the doorway, a man's voice steady and distant — but Werner was not following it. He had the posture of listening without the attention. His eyes were on the floor somewhere between himself and the stove, and his hands were on his knees, opened and not quite resting. She had seen him like this more often lately, sitting alongside the radio without attending to it, the way you sit in a room where you know what you used to do there and have forgotten what that was.

She drew her hand out of the coat pocket.

She looked at the coat on the hook.

If he were to go through the pockets looking for something — his lighter, a key, anything he thought she might have borrowed — he would find it before he found anything else.

She went upstairs.

---

Her room was cold. The grey last light from the window was enough. She sat on the edge of the bed and unfolded the note in her lap.

She knew it by heart, the way you know a thing you have gone back to too many times. Still she read it. She moved through the conscription sentences and the line about the cattle — *das ist keine Klage* — and came to the last two.

*Den Mann auf dem Weg habe ich noch in Erinnerung. Er schien einen langen Weg vor sich zu haben.*

And underneath it, remembered from the afternoon in the barn, what Karl had said in the Allgäu dialect before Oakes came back around: that the man was older, quick on his feet, carrying something, heading in the direction of the water. She had taken it for the kind of detail that sticks because it was strange — a man on a road at night in October rain, not expected.

She thought about what she had heard at Atwood's in October, Jess Atwood speaking to her mother, not particularly to Hannah: *they think he came in from inland, is what Tibbetts said. Because of the shoes.* Smooth-soled, Hannah had gathered — not waterproof, not sea-work shoes. A man who had walked somewhere to get to the harbor.

She had heard at school, in November, that there were no papers, or the papers had gotten damaged — she had been half-listening at the time. She was listening to it now, from inside the memory.

Karl's transport from Bangor came down the coastal road past Wilder's Landing and then south into town. The man he had seen — older, fast for his age, carrying something, heading toward the water — would have been on that same stretch of road.

She did not know what this meant. She could feel it pointing toward something without being able to see what was at the end of the pointing. A man on a road in the rain. A man washed up on the breakwater. A night in October she had not been part of, between those two.

She folded the note back along its lines.

She thought about her father's hands on the fence wire this morning, his back turned toward Karl, watching him carry the wire to the lower field.

She thought: if he went through her coat. If he went through her room.

She got up.

---

The old school bag was in the back of the closet, behind the winter coat and the rubber boots she had outgrown two years ago. Canvas, tan, the strap worn to softness at the buckle. She had carried her textbooks in it when she still went to school with any regularity — before the spring and then the summer and then the fall had pulled her away from it, the farm needing more than school could wait for. She took it out and set it on the bed and looked at the inside bottom.

The seam there was a doubled fold of canvas, stitched with heavy factory thread in a burnt orange that had never matched the bag's color. She pressed her finger along it. Three-quarters of an inch of fold, perhaps more. Enough.

She went to the hall closet and took her mother's sewing box down from the shelf. She did not ask. She chose a darning needle — the eye wide, which was what she needed — and a spool of thread. The thread was black. Wrong, but it didn't matter; no one was going to look at the color of a seam.

Back in her room she sat on the bed with the bag across her knees. She threaded the needle in the dim window light, which took longer than it would have with the lamp. She ran her thumbnail along the seam's edge until she found a stretch where the original stitching had loosened slightly from use — not failing, just softened — and pushed the needle through.

The needle was blunt. She had to lean into it.

She worked three inches of the seam open, keeping the original stitches intact so she could press them back. She took the note and unfolded it flat and smoothed it against her knee, pressing the creases down until it lay as straight as it was going to. She worked it in along the inner canvas, easing it between the two folds, pressing it down with her thumb until it lay flat against the bottom. She could barely feel it through the canvas. The thickness of a note, four times folded and then unfolded, was not very much.

She began stitching the seam closed.

Not even — not machine-tight, nothing that would pass close examination for what it was. But enough. She pulled the thread taut each time without puckering the fold. Six stitches and then a seventh, and then she knotted it twice and cut the thread by pulling it sharp against her thumbnail.

She turned the bag over and ran her fingers across the inside bottom — the canvas, the worn inner lining, the slight change in density where the note lay flat.

Nothing visible. She checked with the back of her hand. Nothing. If her father put his hand into the bag he would feel old canvas and that was all.

She sat for a moment with the bag in her lap.

---

Downstairs she hung the school bag on the hook by the staircase, below her coat. Werner's hat was already on the hook, and her mother's good scarf. The bag hung the way it had used to, before everything else began to take the time school had used — as if it had not been away.

She went to the kitchen.

Werner was at the table now, not the radio. He must have turned it off, or it had gone between programs. He sat with his hands flat on the wood in front of him, no glass or plate between them, looking at his hands the way he had looked at Karl carrying the fence wire across the yard: that same quality of attention that was not presence, not the posture of a man who has arrived where he is sitting.

Marta was at the stove with her back to them both.

*Was denkst du, Vater?*

The thought came in German and stayed there. She said nothing.

She took the water glasses from the shelf and set them on the table — her father's, her mother's, her own. Werner did not look up. His hands were on the table, and the school bag was on the hook in the hall, and outside the kitchen window the December dark had come all the way down over the fields.

She sat in her chair and waited for Marta to bring the pot to the table.

The ice came in from the south. By ten o'clock it had a width to it — not frozen through, but a skim at both flanks of the channel, pressing against the granite of the jetty and the base of the number-two marker. Eira sat at the desk with the lamp turned low and watched it through the window. The channel itself ran open and black between the margins of white. The marker stood plumb. The bell had rung once, at eight-thirty, when the first ice shifted against it; since then, nothing.

She had been in the shack since four in the afternoon. When the temperature dropped below what the tide chart predicted and the south flank had begun to skim, she had carried her overnight kit and supper from the cottage and come down. The number-two marker was five seasons old — new enough that she did not entirely trust it in a hard freeze. The old one had held through worse; she had replaced it for maintenance, not failure, which meant she had less evidence for the new one than she would have liked.

She had gone out at 1800 and again at 2200. Both times the flanks had thickened and both times the channel had been open. She had logged each check in the current volume, come back, and eaten at the desk. Owen's coat was buttoned to her collar; her hands went into the pockets between entries. The oil lamp was as low as she could manage and still write. The tide chart showed the predicted low at 0135; she had penciled a note beside it.

Between the 2200 check and midnight there were two hours in which nothing was supposed to change. The temperature had steadied, had stopped dropping somewhere below twenty, and the flanks had probably put on what ice they were going to put on for the night. The predicted low would narrow the open water slightly and press the flanks, but she had enough history with this marker's anchoring to trust it through moderate pressure. The channel was not going to freeze solid. But she was going to watch it anyway.

The shack was very cold and very quiet. She could hear the harbor — the slight sound of water against the granite when the current shifted, the far-off creak of a dock line somewhere in the marina. No other sound. The lamp flame was the only thing moving in the room.

She would go out at midnight.

The shack frame had a sound at night in winter — settling in the cold, quiet when the temperature had steadied. Tonight it had been quiet for two hours. She reached back and took the old volume from the shelf below the stand.

---

The old volume — started in February of 1941, closed out in early November when the last column filled. The current volume was what she wrote in now. The old one sat on the shelf where old volumes went.

She opened it at random. July 1943: her own hand, the familiar left-ward slant, tide report and vessel traffic, a marginal note about the chart tacking. She turned back. March 1942. December 1941. The columns were neat and complete. She turned further.

The pages changed.

Not the paper — the same stock, the same ruled columns — but the hand. Heavier-pressed, the pen held at a steeper angle, so the downstrokes were thicker than hers and the upstrokes finer. Owen had never corrected in the log; his entries went down complete in the first writing, because he set down what had happened and what had happened was settled.

She had learned to read his entries the way you learn a handwriting after enough years — not the words first but the pressure and the angle, the habit of the pen. His downstrokes were weighted; hers ran light. When she had first taken the log in February of 1936, the shift was visible in the columns from a distance — had there been anyone to see it, which there was no one to be; she had been alone in the shack with his log and her pen. She had not tried to match his hand. The record was the record; it did not ask to be a copy of itself.

She did not need to read his entries. She knew them by the feel.

But she turned through them anyway. April 1936: a vessel logged on a clear morning, the name passing under her thumb without taking. June of the same year: a fog week, seven entries each noting reduced visibility at the channel markers, each complete. The winter of 1937: his hurricane entry ran to three-quarters of a page, wind speeds noted at hourly intervals, the Corcoran vessel's mooring line parting at 0200 and the repair completed and timed. He had logged the man going home.

She had gone looking, years ago, for a gap in his record — some storm week or illness winter where the pressure had been too much and an entry had come up short. She had not found one. Not once in the years she had read backward through the old volumes had his record failed to note a thing he had observed. What he observed, he put down.

His standard was not impossible. It was just his.

She turned to November 1933.

---

Her thumb fell between the pages there. The spine had broken slightly from the number of times she had opened to this section.

*November 19, 1933. Nor'easter. Wind NE, 45 knots gusting 60. Channel: closed 2000 hours. Mooring check 0300: all vessels holding. Agnes Louise on mooring; Corcoran vessel; three at south pier.* Owen had listed them all by name, the way he always did. Then below the main entry, in its own block:

*0100 hours. Vessel observed: unlicensed, running without lights, approximately 30 feet, making for the cove from the NE. Heading 280. Speed approx. 6 knots. Vessel identified (subsequent) as J. Cates, lobsterman, Coldwater. Grounds: outside licensed area. Reported to Rockland: 11/21/33.*

Jared Cates. She had looked him up in the older volumes once, years after, wanting to know what the report had cost him. A man with a decent 34-foot vessel, a habit of working the outer banks when the season went badly enough to require it. Owen's report had cost him a week's hauling rights. He had accepted the warning without a formal appeal.

Owen had written it anyway. The thing had happened; the log recorded what happened. A vessel observed was a vessel reported. There was no column in Owen's log for *observed but not entered* — no room in his practice for that distinction.

Eira set the old volume on the desk and looked at the lamp.

---

She went out at midnight.

Clear and still — the cold that comes when the sky goes empty of cloud and the temperature can fall where it wants. She walked the dock with the lantern to the channel head and knelt at the water's edge.

The ice at the flanks was three-quarters of an inch at the granite. The channel between ran open, the tidal current keeping it moving. The marker stood plumb and the bell was still. She straightened and walked back.

Inside she wrote the 0000 hour entry in the current volume: *Marker: holding. Ice: flanks only; three-quarters inch at granite. Channel: open. Temperature: seventeen degrees.* She blotted it and closed the current volume and set it on the stand.

She picked up the old volume again and turned to October 1943.

---

October 3: the full entry. Body found on the seaward face of the breakwater, 0615 hours, approximately 210 feet from the pier head. The sex, the age as she had estimated it, the clothing in order — coat, trousers, shoes, the leather soles and the absence of grip. The call to Rockland, the constable's arrival, the county examiner's at 1330 with a truck and two assistants and a canvas stretcher. She had written it correctly. She had given it what it required: precision, sequence, the observable facts in the order observed.

She read it through now as she had not read it since the Commander's visit in November. The entry said: Body found. Male. Estimated fifty to sixty years. Clothing as follows. Not identified; case closed. She had written all of that correctly and it was all there and it was all true.

The entry was good because the body had been there to describe. What she had observed on October 2 at 2300 was not a body but two figures at distance, in a storm, for a brief time. She could have described what she observed. She had not done so.

It was, she had always thought, a good entry.

Above it: October 2.

The 0600. The 0900. The 1200. The 1630: *Channel: gale conditions. Vessel traffic: suspended. Wind NE, 40 knots, increasing.*

Then: *2300 hours. Weather: NE gale, 35 knots decreasing at first light. Channel: temporarily impaired.*

The gap between the 1630 entry and the 2300 notation sat on the page without calling attention to itself. If you knew to look for a gap, the notation did not fill it. If you did not know to look — if you were a Commander from Rockland reading through with no reason to find one — the column read as a column reads.

She picked up the pen.

She set the nib just below the 2300 notation, in the space where an additional entry would fall, and wrote:

*October 2, 1943. 2300 hours. Weather—*

She stopped.

What came after the dash: *Dock. Male observed, east dock, approximately 2310. Alive. Approximately fifty-five years. European features. Not alone. Second figure present; not clearly seen. Second figure: person I believe I recognized, though I spoke to neither.*

She could not write it now. Writing it now — three months on, in a log that a Commander from Rockland had reviewed and found satisfactory and closed a case on — meant explaining why she had not written it in October. And explaining October meant the choice had a name.

She had told herself it was waiting, not deciding. It was January now.

She drew a line through what she had written. One line, clean, straight — the standard in a legal document; the original words must remain readable beneath it. She could see them through the line: *October 2, 1943. 2300 hours. Weather—* She initialed it: *E.B.* Then she wrote below:

*[Entry error — see correction below.]*

*Ice report, 0015 hours: Number-two marker holding. Ice: flanks, three-quarters inch. Channel: open.*

She dated it. She blotted it. She set the pen on the stand.

---

She looked at what she had done.

The entry was in the record now. Crossed out, initialed, corrected according to procedure — which was how a legal document handled an error. *October 2, 1943. 2300 hours. Weather—* with a line through it and the initials and the correction notice below. Anyone who read this log closely would see the line. They would see what she had started and not finished. They would not know what came after *Weather—* because she had not written it. But they would know there had been an entry attempted and set aside.

Owen's 1933 entry was thirty pages back, unaltered.

She set the old volume on the shelf. Owen's pages were there. She was not Owen. She had known this since January 1936, when she sat at this desk for the first time — the post and the log all his, carried over to her by the selectman who had been embarrassed to ask a woman and more embarrassed by the others who had declined. She had kept the record eight years. She knew what she had kept and what she had not.

She was not Owen.

It was just past midnight.

She moved her chair to face the window. The channel lay between its white flanks — the open water darker than the ice on either side. The cold came in around the door frame, the same draft it always came in, and the lamp flame bent toward it and then straightened. She put her hands in Owen's pockets.

Three hours until the next check.

The harbor was quiet. The ice was doing what it was doing. She had done what she was going to do tonight and not done what she was not going to do. The lamp burned. The cold held at what it had settled to.

She thought about nothing in particular. She sat.

---

She went out at four.

The ice had not crossed. The channel ran open between the flanks and the marker stood plumb and the bell was still. She knelt on the granite and checked the flank thickness — no thicker than at midnight, possibly thinner at the low-water line where the tide had pushed under it in the night. She stood. The harbor was completely still.

She walked back to the shack and wrote the 0400 entry in the current volume. Temperature, wind — none — channel, ice: *flanks only; channel open; marker: holding.*

---

In January the light came after seven. She sat at the desk with the lamp turned down and waited. The window showed nothing for a long time and then showed the harbor emerging from the dark — water first, a grey movement between the banks, then the far bank itself, the boathouse roof against the beginning sky, the fields beyond it. The ice at the flanks showed white in the first light, two margins of white with the black channel running between. The marker held. The bell was still.

She wrote the morning report. Date, temperature, wind, channel, ice: *flanks only; channel open; marker: holding.*

She closed the current volume and set it on the stand. The old volume was on the shelf below it. The crossed-out entry was in it — correct in its form, visible to anyone who looked closely at October 2.

She put on her coat and went out to check the tide.
