# Chapter 8 — Montreal

The school was empty except for him from eight until noon. He had carried the materials over in the briefcase: the second-year Latin quiz, two composition prompts for the German class, a reading passage adapted from a newspaper text dated to the spring of 1940, which was old enough by now to be permissible in the current circumstances. The policy was not written down but Marcus had read it correctly without being told. He sharpened the pencils in the German room's window crock — a Saturday habit of some months' standing — and spread his notes on the desk and spent two hours drafting quiz questions.

The school produced a particular kind of quiet when the students were absent: different from a library's quiet, different from an empty house. A building designed for forty people at a time held the residue of its ordinary noise in the walls, the corridors, the arrangement of the desks. He found it easier to think in this quiet than in most others available to him. He could hear himself clearly here without the accompanying sense that someone was watching him hear himself.

He drank two cups of coffee from the percolator in the custodian's room. Henry was not in on Saturdays; the percolator ran until whatever time Henry turned it off on Friday afternoons, and it was still on when Marcus arrived at eight. He had been availing himself of this for several months without mentioning it.

He locked the school at noon, came down the front steps, and turned up Prospect Street into the March wind. The quality of the cold had changed in the past two weeks — not warmer but different in its character, the structural cold of deep winter giving way to something thinner, a cold that had conceded its argument without quite leaving. The mud at the road's edge had been frozen solid since December and was now beginning not to be. Bare dirt showed along the south side of the Dunbar fence where the snowpack had thinned. He walked with his collar up and came to the Crow house on the right.

He came in the front door and set the briefcase against the wall.

Lillian was in the kitchen — a drawer pulled open, and then water from the tap, and then quiet. The hallway table held the day's mail: a circular from Atwood's, an envelope bearing the telephone company's mark, and one other piece of mail, set slightly apart from the other two.

He stopped.

A plain white envelope. The return address in the upper left was a suite number on a street in Montreal he did not recognize — the correct caution; Ehrlich would not send from his own address on an envelope going through the American domestic post. The postmark read *Montréal, P.Q.* The date: February 26.

Three weeks in transit. He had addressed and mailed his own letter in the second week of February — an early Saturday morning, before Henry came downstairs, the house quiet, a four-minute walk to the post-box on Prospect Street. He had put the envelope in the box before he had stood there long enough to reconsider the matter. Three weeks from that morning to this.

He took the letter upstairs.

---

His room had the smell of the lamp and the still cold of a room whose radiator had been cycling down since Thursday, when the furnace grate had started to partially block. He sat at the desk without taking off his coat. The envelope opened on ordinary gum.

The letter was two pages, written on good commercial stationery in a hand he recognized: German cursive corrected toward English legibility, the descenders held close, the capitals moderate, the overall impression of a man who had learned to write in one system and was disciplined enough, writing in another language, to remain readable. Ehrlich had always written to him in English. This was the practice between them, established in their first years of correspondence — when correspondence had been possible without the weight it now carried.

*Dear Dr. Klein,*

*Thank you for your letter of the third. I was glad to receive news of your situation in Maine.*

*Regarding your inquiry about German-language reading texts for secondary school use: I would recommend, if obtainable, the Diesterweg graded readers, which were widely used in German schools through the late thirties and are pedagogically sound. Some stock may still be available through the academic book trade in Toronto. The Langenscheidt intermediate series is another possibility; I believe a Montreal supplier carries current stock, and I can provide the contact if it would be useful.*

*I was glad to hear from you in other respects as well. It has been some time.*

*As to the Josef Lutz you mention: I knew him from Sherbrooke, yes. He was released — if my recollection is correct — in November of 1942, some months after I had left myself; he was still in the block when I was discharged. He had a cousin in New York, in the garment district, whom he had been trying to reach for a considerable time. This was still his intention when I last saw him. I know that he left this city in the first days of September of last year, as I helped him with certain of the practical details of the departure, the nature of which I will not set down in a letter. His contacts here and I had expected to hear from him by November at the latest. We have not heard.*

*I had hoped he had simply lost touch. These things happen. If you have heard anything of him, I would be grateful to know it.*

*With regards,*
*S. Ehrlich*

He read it twice. He set it on the desk.

---

The structure of what Ehrlich's letter said, set out in order:

Josef had left Montreal in the first days of September 1943. Ehrlich had helped with the practical details of the departure — which meant, as a matter of inference from what letters of this kind could and could not specify, documents of some kind, a route, possibly money, because organizations of the type Ehrlich ran seldom had money to distribute beyond what each case required, and they weighed cases against one another according to an accounting Marcus could imagine in its categories if not its specific arithmetic. For a man without valid papers and without an American visa, the route south from Montreal to New York did not run directly. It ran east into New England first, along the roads that crossed the Quebec border without much scrutiny, and then south through Maine along the coast, through whatever arrangements obtained in the coastal towns — the kind of arrangements that were available to people who knew the right names and were trusted with them. And then New York at the far end of it.

Six weeks minimum for such a route, traveling carefully and resting where shelter was available. Eight weeks at the outside.

September plus six weeks: mid-October. September plus eight weeks: the first of November.

The body had come in against the breakwater on the morning of October 3, 1943.

This was not certainty. It was an argument from four independently sourced facts — the departure date from Ehrlich, the route from the geography, the indication of destination and timing from the fragment's text (*ankommen*, to arrive; *nicht mehr warten*, can wait no longer), and the date from the newspaper account Marcus had read in the school library the previous October, which had said: *unidentified man, October 1943, found on the Coldwater Reach breakwater following a three-day gale.* Four sources for one conclusion did not produce certainty. They made the distance between the argument and certainty short enough that the distinction had ceased to carry practical weight. He had been treating it as certainty since November; Ehrlich's letter confirmed what he had already concluded, with the fixed departure date added and one further dimension he had not fully accounted for: the waiting. Ehrlich and his contacts in Montreal had been expecting word since November. They had not received any. *I had hoped he had simply lost touch.*

It was March. He had not simply lost touch.

Marcus opened the bottom drawer of the desk. The fragment was face-down under the manila folder where it had been since October. He lifted the folder and turned the fragment over: the brown shadows of the dissolved ink, the heading block with its partial address. *...Lutz, J...* He set Ehrlich's letter on the desk beside the fragment, face-up — the found object and the received reply, the one that had arrived from the sea and the one that had arrived from the post-box on Prospect Street. He looked at them for a moment. Then he placed the manila folder over both of them and closed the drawer.

---

At Sherbrooke, in the B-block, the men had organized a lending arrangement for whatever reading material came through the compound gates. Someone kept a notebook; the books and pamphlets and periodicals were tracked and distributed, and returned when finished, and tracked again. Josef had come to the lending table every two weeks and borrowed everything in German. It did not matter what — the theological tracts, the primer for English-speakers learning German as a foreign language, which Josef did not need and read anyway, perhaps for the particular pleasure of reading something familiar in a form organized for someone who had never known it, the water-stained Fontane novel that had been circulating through the block since spring. He read in the evenings with his back to the wall and his lamp at its highest setting, which was not very high, and he read with the specific attention of a man who is not certain about the next book. Not anxious — specific. He handled the volumes carefully; he returned them without damage. He was an archivist by training and there was something in the way he held a borrowed book — the care with the spine, the way he turned pages from the corner rather than the edge — that could not entirely be trained out of his hands even when the book in question had no particular value and would have survived rougher handling.

He had said once, in the third winter, in German: *The problem with travel is that it is incompatible with libraries.* He had said it as a complaint with a joke inside it. Marcus had laughed.

A man with that habit, moving south from Montreal with whatever Ehrlich's practical details could arrange — he would not have gone without books. One volume, perhaps two. The papers he could not abandon, and the books beside the papers in the same bundle, the same weight carried because it was the only kind of weight worth carrying. Both in the bundle when he came down the coastal road in October in the rain.

Marcus put his coat on the chair. He sat on the edge of the bed.

The radiator ticked once and did not tick again.

From downstairs came the sound of Lillian in the kitchen.

---

At six he went downstairs.

Lillian had made potatoes with salt pork worked through them and dried parsley from the autumn kitchen garden — a ration-book meal in the way of most meals now, the meat distributed through the vegetables rather than present as its own fact, filling and correct in its intentions. Henry was already at the table with his hands folded on the placemat, his newspaper set to the side. From the next room the radio carried the evening news in an even voice — something about the Pacific, the announcer reading from a prepared text without particular urgency.

Marcus sat. He served himself. He ate.

"Furnace grate," Henry said. "I'll look at it Monday."

"I was in my coat at the desk all morning."

"Monday," Henry said.

They ate. Lillian served herself and sat without remark about the meal; she was not a woman who performed satisfaction with food, and Marcus had found this quality restful over the months of eating at this table. The food was the food. They were eating it. The radio shifted from news to a program of music sometime in the middle of the meal, and Henry reached around the doorframe without getting up and turned the dial down. The quiet of the house settled in behind the sound of forks on plates.

After a while the table was cleared.

---

Marcus went upstairs and came back with the composition exercises and spread them at the corner of the table. Henry moved to the armchair; Lillian went to the kitchen. The lamp at the table's center threw a steady light across the papers.

The exercises were from the first-year class: twelve sentences in English rendered into Latin, or attempted. Four had not been attempted; he marked these as blanks, not as errors — a student who understood the limits of their knowledge and declined to guess had made a reasonable accounting. Of the eight attempts, the errors fell into the predictable range: case endings confused under certain prepositions, the subjunctive absent where the construction required it, one student in the consistent habit of declining the second declension as if it belonged to the third. He marked each error in red pencil. He wrote the correct form small in the margin beside the wrong one, so that when the student got the paper back they could see both forms adjacent — the one they had written and the one the sentence wanted.

Henry's newspaper turned in the armchair. From the kitchen came the sound of cups placed in the drying rack, one at a time, and then the water turned off, and then the quieter sound of Lillian putting something away in the far cabinet.

He corrected the genitive in the sixth exercise — *amico* where *amici* was wanted, a confusion between the dative and the genitive that was common in the first year and would not, in most students, survive the second — wrote the form in the margin, and moved to the seventh.

# Chapter 9 — The Road

The harness wanted sorting, and Karl was doing it: collar from collar, the throatlatch lines unwound from where they'd gathered through the winter, each piece held briefly and appraised and set on the appropriate nail or left on the bench for a second pass. He worked with the same unhurry he worked everything, and Hannah had been watching him for two weeks now — from across the yard, over a fence rail, from the farmhouse window above the kitchen sink — and she had known, watching, that the sorting was not what she was waiting for.

The wagon shed door stood open across the yard. Oakes had carried his flask over at half past two, moving with the slow care of a man whose knees had their opinions about the cold. She had watched him cross. She had not seen him come out.

Werner was in the upper field with the other three. She had watched him go up the hill at noon.

She picked up the feed bucket from beside the tack room door and walked into the corridor.

Karl looked up when she came in. His hands didn't stop — they found the buckle they'd been reaching toward and set it on the bench — but he looked at her and the looking was a full sentence, the kind that didn't need words to say what it said.

She came in far enough for the barn to close around her. The smell of the winter still lived here: old hay, the cold that kept itself in the boards long after the air outside had shifted, the particular breath of the milk cows below. Outside, along the south fence, the snow had pulled back and the dark mud had come up in long tongues. In the upper field the other three were moving between fence posts, Werner among them, his back toward the barn.

She set the bucket down. She did not pick up anything else.

Karl's hands were quiet on the bench.

The silence between them had a texture. She had learned, over these weeks, that Karl's silences were not nervous — they were a kind of patience, an economy her father's silences had the same quality of, though she would not have said this to either of them. She stood, and he waited, and outside a crow called once from the direction of the upper pasture and did not call again.

"Ich hab' etwas," she said. *I have something.*

He waited.

She had opened the bag seam the night before, by the lamp in her room. The sewing scissors, the blade turned sidewise, the black thread cut one stitch at a time so the canvas didn't pucker. Six stitches and then the seventh came with them, and she had pulled the note out flat and looked at it under the lamp — his handwriting, the four folds, the pencil lines slightly silvered under the lamplight — and then she had folded it back into its four folds and set it in her coat pocket. She had lain awake for a while after that, listening to Werner's radio come through the floor.

She had carried the note in her pocket all through the morning, through the first milking and the hay and the carrying of things that needed carrying. It had pressed through the fabric when she moved.

She reached into her coat pocket now and took it out.

She held it toward him with his side facing him. His handwriting — the Allgäu hand, the pencil-pressed letters she had read often enough to know without reading.

He looked at the note in her hand. He looked at her. He didn't take it.

"Das hier," she said. "Der Mann auf dem Weg. Erzähl mir davon."

*This. The man on the road. Tell me.*

She kept her voice level — the level that meant nothing to someone listening for a particular language, the level she used for German that was not meant to be German from across a yard. The barn corridor was not private: Werner could come back through the upper door, Oakes could round the corner from the wagon shed. But the flask was across the yard and Werner was in the upper field and these were the minutes she had.

Karl looked once toward the open barn door, toward the light of the April yard. Then he looked back at her. She could see him deciding — not whether to speak but how, the same care that had gone into the note in the first place, the care of a person who understood that words, once out, couldn't be called back.

He pulled a length of leather from the pile on the bench and began working it through his hands — the motion of someone doing something while saying something else.

"Ein Donnerstag," he said. "Oder Freitag. Anfang Oktober." *A Thursday. Or Friday. Early in October.*

She was still holding the note.

"Der Truck kam von Bangor zurück." *The truck was coming back from Bangor.* His voice stayed low and even; his eyes stayed on the leather. "Wir hatten einen Auftrag in einer Konservenfabrik, den ganzen Tag. Auf dem Rückweg hat es geregnet — den ganzen Abend schon, schlechte Straßen." *We had an assignment at a cannery, the whole day. On the way back it had been raining — all evening, the roads were bad.*

She knew about the cannery runs: Oakes had mentioned it once, in passing, the way he mentioned things he considered procedural fact and not conversation. October, early in the month, before the winter reduction had come.

"Bei Wilder's Landing," Karl said — *at Wilder's Landing* — "lag ein Ast auf dem Weg. Groß genug, dass der Fahrer langsamer gemacht hat." *there was a branch across the road. Large enough that the driver slowed down.*

The Landing. She had driven past it with her father perhaps a dozen times in daylight: a wide curve in the coastal road where the white pines overhung the verge and you could see a long way south on clear days, toward where the town lights would be. At night, in October rain, through the window of a transport truck — the headlamps would reach only so far, and beyond them the dark and the trees and whatever was on the road.

"Auf der linken Seite," Karl said. "Durch das Fenster — ein Mann zu Fuß." *On the left side. Through the window — a man on foot.*

He was quiet for a moment, not for effect but genuinely placing himself back in that cab, in the wet and the dark and the branch in the headlamps.

"Wie alt?" she said. *How old?*

He considered. "Älter als ich. Vielleicht fünfzig. Vielleicht ein bisschen mehr." *Older than me. Perhaps fifty. Perhaps a little more.* "Schmächtig. Kein Bauer — das konnte man sehen, auch in dem Regen." *Slight. Not a farmer's build — you could see that, even in the rain.*

Not from here, then. The shape of something she had been carrying since December began to settle against his words, the way a fit you weren't expecting turns out to be exactly right.

"Er trug etwas," Karl said. "Eine Tasche, oder ein Bündel — er hielt es nah am Körper, schwer zu erkennen im Regen." *He was carrying something. A bag, or a bundle — he held it close to his body, hard to make out in the rain.*

She thought about smooth-soled shoes. What Jess Atwood had said at the counter in November, relaying Tibbetts: *came from inland, you could tell by the shoes.* She thought about the note in her hand and the four folds of it and what was written in the last two lines.

"Er hatte einen langen Mantel," Karl said. *He had a long coat.* "Nicht so einen für den Regen. Einen Stadtmantel." *Not one for the weather. A city coat.*

Not a fisherman's coat. Not an oilskin.

"Er ging in Richtung Wasser."

*He was moving toward the water.*

He let that sit. She let it sit with him. Outside, the April yard was quiet — the scratch of a branch somewhere against the upper barn's east wall, the distant sound of Werner's voice to one of the others in the field.

"Ich hatte vielleicht zehn Sekunden," Karl said. "Wegen des Astes hat der Fahrer gebremst und dann sofort weitergemacht." *I had perhaps ten seconds. Because of the branch the driver braked and then moved on immediately.*

Ten seconds of a rain-fogged window on an October night. Enough. She thought: enough to see what he was and where he was going.

"Und dann," Karl said — and there was a particular quality to the pause before it, the pause of a thing said for the first time — "hat er sich umgedreht. Er hat den Truck gesehen. Direkt hineingeschaut, durch den Regen." *And then — he turned around. He looked at the truck. Looked directly at it, through the rain.*

She waited.

"Und ist einfach weitergelaufen." *And just kept walking.*

He had not stopped. Had not flagged the truck, not moved toward the road's center, not raised his arm. He had looked at the headlamps coming through the rain and turned back and kept on, moving in the direction of the water, at the pace of a man going somewhere.

Going somewhere. She held on to that.

Karl set the length of leather down on the bench. He was looking at the barn floor now, at the boards that had held horses and cattle and men's boots through decades she couldn't number.

"War es der Mann?" he said, quietly. *Was it that man?*

He meant the one. The one with the smooth-soled shoes and no papers and no name on the stone in the town cemetery. He had put it together from her questions or from her face or from the fact of the feed bucket she didn't need; she couldn't have said which. He had put it together and he was looking at her and he was nineteen years old and he had written those two sentences in November and pressed the note into her palm and he had known then, she thought, in the way you know things you can't say.

"Ich glaube schon," she said. *I think so.*

He absorbed this without moving. He didn't look away from her, and she didn't look away from him. There was something in his stillness that she recognized from the night she had first read the note — the quality of someone who has been carrying a thing for a while and now has set it down, not into safety but into the world, where it would have weight in a way it hadn't had before.

"Was denkst du, was passiert ist?" he said. *What do you think happened?*

She opened her mouth and closed it.

She thought about the ten seconds at Wilder's Landing, the man looking at the headlamps through the rain and then turning away and continuing on his own direction. She thought about the harbor, which she had not seen herself but had heard about from Jess Atwood's cousin's wife the following week: the gale that had started that night or the next morning and the body on the breakwater seaward face at 0615. Between a man walking with purpose toward the water and the body found in the morning — that distance was not something she could close. She did not know who was at the dock or what the dock had looked like that night or what had happened between his arriving there and his not leaving.

"Ich weiß es nicht," she said.

She meant it.

He nodded once, a single slow dip of his head, and reached for the harness buckle again.

---

Across the yard: boots on the wagon shed threshold, the familiar sound — a flat first step, a heavier second step where Oakes's right knee found the drop.

Karl was already working. She picked up the feed bucket.

By the time Oakes came around the corner of the barn she was tipping grain into the nearest bin, the dry sound of it filling the corridor, and Karl had a collar on the right nail and was reaching for the next.

Oakes looked in at them. He pulled the front of his coat together against the April wind, which still had winter in it this close to the water.

"Cold today," he said.

"Ja," Karl said, without looking up.

Oakes moved on, toward the lower gate, his boots loud on the mud.

Hannah set the empty bucket down. She didn't look at Karl and he didn't look at her. She picked up the bucket and walked out of the barn and across the yard toward the milk house, the note in her coat pocket pressing through the fabric in its four folds, and she carried it the way she had learned to carry it — as a plain fact about the day, neither more nor less.

---

Marta had gone to bed early, headache reaching up from the back of her neck in the way that meant the next morning too. Werner was in the parlor with the radio, the sound of it coming through the wall, words she had stopped listening to. He had been sitting that way most evenings — not attending to the radio, she thought, only needing it there the way you need a lamp in a room you're not using.

She washed the supper dishes and stacked them in the rack and wiped down the table and then sat at it. She turned the lamp down and then up one notch, to the right level for close work.

She took the note out of her coat pocket and set it on the table.

Karl's writing face up: the four paragraphs, the pencil lines faintly silvered in the lamplight, the Allgäu spelling of certain words she had stopped noticing long ago — *daheim* for home, the particular way he wrote his r's so they came down from the top. She had read it enough times that she could have said the words without seeing them. She looked at it for a moment and then turned it over.

The other side was blank.

She got up and went to the parlor drawer where Marta kept the spare pencils and brought one back. She sat. The blank side of the note was small-ruled — the lines faintly blue-gray in the lamplight, the kind of paper from a workbook, the kind of paper that turned up in a POW camp's limited supply and was used for whatever needed to be written. She looked at it for a moment.

Then she began to write.

Her own hand: lighter-pressed than Karl's, the way her teacher had shown her for keeping the point fine on a soft pencil. Small letters, even — she wanted everything legible, wanted no excuse for misreading later. German, because it was the right language for what she was doing. The language her father had said was the language of exactness: you said what you meant, you meant what you said, you didn't put in what wasn't there.

*Wilder's Landing, Küstenstraße.* The place first, the way you began a proper account.

*Oktober 1943 — Donnerstag oder Freitag, nachts, gegen zehn oder elf.* October 1943, Thursday or Friday, nighttime, around ten or eleven.

She wrote what Karl had told her. She wrote it in order, the facts as they had come: *Einen Mann zu Fuß auf der linken Straßenseite.* A man on foot on the left side of the road. *Älter. Schmächtig. Einen langen Mantel, nicht für das Wetter — einen Stadtmantel.* Older. Slight. A long coat, not for the weather — a city coat. *Trug etwas, ein Bündel oder eine Tasche, nah am Körper gehalten.* Carrying something, a bundle or a bag, held close to the body.

She paused. She wrote: *Bewegte sich Richtung Wasser.*

She wrote it and it was as exact as she could make it, which was all she had to offer it.

*Sah sich um — schaute den Truck direkt an, durch den Regen.*

Turned to look — looked directly at the truck, through the rain.

*Lief weiter.*

Kept walking.

That was Karl's account. She had written it down in the order he had given it, without adding to it or taking anything from it. She set the pencil down.

She looked at what she had written.

Then she picked up the note in both hands.

His writing on one side, hers on the other. His in November; hers tonight, in April, at the kitchen table with the supper things put away and the lamplight low. His four paragraphs about himself — Marktoberdorf, the conscription, the cattle that reminded him of home, the man on the road he still remembered — and on the other side her lines about the man on the road, where he had been, what he had been doing, what Karl had seen in the ten seconds before the truck moved on.

Two sides. Two hands. Two moments.

She held the note and felt the weight of it — the small-ruled paper, barely larger than what you could cup between two palms, both sides filled now. In the parlor the radio talked in its even voice about something in the Pacific. Werner's chair was still.

She had thought she knew what she was holding. In November under the lamp, in December at the bag lining: she had thought she understood the note, what it was, what it meant for her to have it. She had been wrong. What she had understood then was a note from a boy who had seen something on a road in the rain and written it down because it had been sitting in him without a place to go.

What she held now was the last known account of a man who had been alive and walking under his own power at Wilder's Landing on a night in early October 1943, heading toward the harbor, and had been found on the breakwater in the morning. Karl had been in the truck. She had written it down. Both their hands were in this paper, in this kitchen, in this house, and as far as she could determine, no one else had been on that road at that hour who had seen what Karl had seen.

She folded the note.

She put it in her coat pocket. She would put it back in the bag tomorrow, sew the seam back. Tonight it needed to be where she could feel it.

In the parlor Werner shifted once in his chair and was still again.

Hannah set both hands flat on the table and looked at the lamplight on the wood and did not move them.

input.summary: Late March / early April 1944. The POW crew has been back since the first of March; Hannah has been waiting two weeks for a window. On a Wednesday afternoon, Oakes takes his flask to the wagon shed at half past two; Werner is in the upper field with the other three. Hannah goes into the barn corridor with a feed bucket she doesn't need. Karl is sorting harness alone. After a silence, she shows him the note — his side facing him — and asks in German: Das hier. Der Mann auf dem Weg. Erzähl mir davon. Karl tells her: an early October night, Thursday or Friday, the Bangor transport returning in the rain. At Wilder's Landing a branch across the road slowed the truck. On the left side of the road: a man on foot. Älter. Schmächtig. Einen langen Mantel — a city coat, not an oilskin. Carrying something held close. Moving toward the water. The truck slowed perhaps ten seconds; in those ten seconds the man turned, looked directly at the truck through the rain, and kept walking. Going somewhere. Karl asks: War es der Mann? Hannah: Ich glaube schon. He asks what she thinks happened. She says: Ich weiß es nicht. She means it — she knows where he was going; not what happened at the dock. Oakes's boots on the wagon shed threshold end the scene; they are working when he rounds the corner. That evening: Marta in bed with a headache, Werner at the radio not attending. Hannah sits at the kitchen table alone, takes the note out, turns it over to the blank side, and writes Karl's account in German — small, careful letters, fact by fact. Wilder's Landing, Küstenstraße. Oktober 1943. The description. Bewegte sich Richtung Wasser. Sah sich um. Lief weiter. She folds the note and holds it — both sides — and understands what she is holding: the only account of the last known sighting of a man found dead the next morning. Both their hands in the paper. She puts it in her coat pocket for tonight and will sew it back in the bag tomorrow.

# Chapter 10 — No New Information

The form had been under the log for a week. She had put it there on the Thursday it arrived—folded inside the larger Rockland envelope along with two vessel-movement notices—and had not taken it out again until now.

She sat at the desk. The lamp was burning though the morning light from the east window was sufficient; she had lit it at six and not blown it out. Outside, the harbor lay in the grey of an overcast April morning, the water running with the spring chop, the mooring buoy at the channel bend turning in the tidal draw. Agnes Louise was on the inner mooring. The east channel was clear.

She had until the fifteenth. Today was the thirteenth.

She took the form out from under the log and set it on the desk.

One page. *Office of the District Commander, First Naval District, Rockland, Maine.* Printed letterhead, a case stamp at the upper right: *Follow-Up Inquiry — Case No. CLD-43-081.* The case number was the one from the October filing, which she had entered in the log's reference column when Rockland's acknowledgment had come back. Below the letterhead, three sections, each with a ruled blank line:

*Date of original finding.*
*Location of finding.*
*Cause of death as determined by county examiner.*

Then:

*New witnesses, physical evidence, or information bearing on identity or cause of death:*

And at the bottom: *Signature and date. Return by: April 15, 1944.*

She opened the log to October.

The spine gave at October without pressing—she had turned to these pages twice in winter and the binding had learned them. The page showed October 2 at the top: the 2300 weather notation, which she had written before she went down to the dock. *Weather: NE gale, 35 knots decreasing at first light. Channel: temporarily impaired.* Below it, on the same page: the crossed-out line. Her own hand, a single stroke through it, the initials E.B. in the margin, the correction notice and the 0015 ice report below that. She had written those in January during the ice watch. She did not read the crossed-out line now. She turned forward one page to October 3.

The body entry. She had written it in the early morning of the third, between Tibbetts's first call and the county examiner's arrival. She read it through. It was a good entry—complete in every particular. Time of discovery: 0615. Location: *seaward face, approximately 210 feet from pier head.* Description: *male, estimated fifty to sixty years. Heavy dark wool overcoat; wool trousers; leather-soled shoes, smooth, no grip. No papers of any kind.* Cause of death as later determined by county examiner: *undetermined drowning.* Signed E. Bowman, initialed A. Tibbetts.

She copied what she needed onto the form. October 3, 1943. Seaward face, 210 feet from pier head. Undetermined drowning. She copied exactly, without alteration. The pen moved steadily. The facts did not change with the copying.

Then: *New witnesses, physical evidence, or information bearing on identity or cause of death.*

She wrote: *None.*

She set the pen down.

She looked at the word. Then she picked the form up and read it through from the top.

The date was right. The location was right. The examiner's language was copied exactly.

She held the form and moved through what she had. The same order she used for a channel checklist: one item at a time, no skipping.

October 2, 1943. The east dock. Twenty-three hundred and ten hours, approximately—she had not checked the watch when she left the shack but it had read 2308 on the desk, and the dock was fifty yards. The gale had been building since mid-afternoon; cloud cover solid by 2100, the wind clocking east-northeast and increasing. The dock lamp at the seaward end had gone dark sometime after twenty-two hundred. She had noted it on her 2200 circuit and had not replaced the bulb because the ladder in that wind was inadvisable and it was not an emergency. She had gone to the east dock on the mooring circuit because something had moved.

The man had been alive. Standing upright, not slumped, not in distress she could see. She had registered him from thirty or forty feet—the shape of him in the poor light, the weight of his coat in the wind, the way he shifted his weight from foot to foot in the way of someone waiting rather than someone who had fallen or been struck. A long coat, dark wool, heavy. Not an oilskin.

Not from here. She had known the bodies of the harbor's men for eight years—their particular weight, the posture of men who worked the water or the fields, the way they stood in weather. This one was none of those. Something about the coat or the stance or the way he had turned when she first noticed him: European, she had thought. She had not gone close enough to be certain. The light was poor and the wind was building and she had stopped at the dock's edge.

He was not alone.

A second figure was standing to his left, ten or twelve feet away. She had seen the height and the way the weight sat—the particular arrangement of the shoulders, the particular way of standing with the weight slightly forward—and had thought, in that moment: someone from here. Someone whose shape she had encountered somewhere in the ordinary course of the town's days. She had not been able to put a name to it. The dark; the distance; the wind.

She had not spoken to either of them. She had stood at the dock's edge long enough to see what she had seen and then had turned and walked back to the shack and had made no entry.

By 0615 he was against the seaward face.

She set the form down.

*None.* The word sat on the Rockland letterhead without apology. No new witnesses had come forward to her office. No new physical evidence had been submitted. No information bearing on the examiner's determination had been received in her official capacity.

She folded the form along its three original creases. She fitted it into the envelope—the District return address already printed at the upper left—and ran the gum strip along the back of her tongue and sealed it.

The envelope lay on the desk beside the log. Two documents with her name on them, each covering October 2. One of them covered it with a line of weather and a crossed-out attempt. The other covered it with a word.

She took her coat from the back of the door and put the envelope in her pocket.

---

Outside, the harbor was running.

Two boats had gone before five—she had heard the engines from the cottage before first light—and a third had cleared the channel at half past seven, the Beaumont forty-footer that had docked in Sunday evening. The spring grounds were opening; several of the winter-idle boats had gone out in the last two weeks and not yet come back. The mooring field was thinner than it would be by June—three vessels down in Rockland for bottom work—and the channel had that clean look it got in early spring, before the summer traffic filled it in. The buoy at the channel bend was turning steadily in the tidal draw.

She walked the access road up the bluff. The mud at the road's edges had not crusted yet; she took the center. The roadside ditches on the south side were down to a trickle, the snowmelt finished, and the grass along the verge was still winter-flat but beginning to show color at the root. The air was cold with the honest cold of a coast in April—diesel and seawater and under them the turned-earth smell from somewhere inland, the farms beginning to plow. The light was flat and partial, the overcast thinning in places but not breaking.

She passed Atwood's. The door was open; someone inside, a voice she did not place. The church steps were empty. The war notice board outside the church had two new names since she had last looked, pinned with the paper tabs Willard Oakes cut from the cardstock he kept under the post office counter. She did not stop to read them.

The post office was in the brick building past the church. A bell on the door. Mrs. Welliver was behind the counter with the incoming tray.

She looked up. "Morning."

"Morning. For the outgoing."

"Morning pick-up's gone. This'll go with the two-thirty."

"That's fine."

Eira set the envelope on the counter. She did not wait for it to be taken.

---

She did not take the direct road back.

The access road ran down the bluff to the breakwater's landward end, and the shack was a five-minute walk from there. She had come by that road this morning. She had gone to the breakwater's mid-point twice over the winter—once to check the forty-foot navigation light after a complaint from the Loomis boat, once without a stated errand—and both times she had stopped at the mid-point and gone back.

Today she walked to the end.

The granite was wet with spray. A stone in the fourth course near the pier head had lifted slightly in the winter freeze—she had reported it to Rockland in February, flagged it in the maintenance log, not yet heard back. It was not dangerous; she stepped around it. The pier-head housing for the navigation beacon stood dark, as it would until dusk. The iron railing on the channel side was furred with salt.

Below: the seaward face.

The spring tidal flush had turned the water grey-green and turbid, the bottom material from the winter storms still working up. The channel ran south through the passage and the tidal draw showed as a slight corrugation in the surface—the pattern of deep water moving at pace. Cold still; the sea did not warm in April. The northeast wind came in off the open water at twelve knots or so, steady, and the spray reached her intermittently.

She looked down at the seaward face.

The outer course of the granite sat slightly proud of the inner, the way it had always sat—not design, just settlement over the years of frost and load—and made a concavity at water level that caught the backwash in storm weather. In the three-day blow last October the foam would have climbed to the third or fourth course. Now the water worked at the stone with the ordinary persistence of spring and the concavity was clear. The barnacles ran heavy from winter. The kelp had started in the lower angle, dark green and moving with the current. A length of fouled line had lodged in the upper angle sometime in the last week, tangled around the old ring bolt; she made a note to send Noss to clear it.

The harbor behind her was quiet in the early-afternoon way, the outgoing boats out on the grounds and the incomings not yet in sight. The wind was in her ears. The water moved below.

She stood for a time with her boots close to the stone's edge and looked at the seaward face and the water working at it.

Then she turned and walked back along the granite.

---

She made the afternoon log entry at quarter to five.

Tide height at 1417: eleven feet two inches above chart datum. Wind northwest, variable, ten to twelve knots. Weather: improving; the fog advisory had lifted at 1100, which she had logged at the time and carried forward now. One vessel movement since the morning: the Beaumont forty-footer docking at 1623, inbound from Rockland.

She read the entry through.

All columns accounted for.

She closed the log.

The oil lamp made its steady light on the desk. The afternoon was failing—the sun past the bluff, the east window showing the harbour sky going grey at the horizon, the water below it darkening. The lamp's circle fell on the desk surface, the log's worn cover, the pen in its groove beside the inkstand. The shack was quiet.

She put her hands in her lap.

Outside, the harbour ran.

# Chapter 11 — The Crow Table

The walk home from the school took twelve minutes at ordinary pace — up Prospect Street from the building's front steps, past the intersection at Dunbar, past the Welliver house and the elm that overhung the corner-lot fence, and to the Crow house on the right.

In May the walk was different from what it had been in March. The light came in at a lower angle now and reached the full width of the street in the late afternoon, and the air had a layered quality he did not try to name, the structural cold of a long winter conceded but not yet gone, the warmth of something gathering underneath it. The mud at the road's edge had been solid since before January and was no longer solid. He walked with his coat open. He came through the gate at the Crow house — the latch giving with its familiar slight resistance, the same resistance it had had since the September afternoon in 1942 when Henry had shown him the room and asked no further questions about the Quaker organization or about why a language teacher from Vienna had come by way of Paris, London, and a camp in Quebec to a fishing town on the Maine coast — and he went up the front walk and came through the door.

Lillian was in the kitchen. He knew this before he heard her. The house had a different smell than it had on ordinary evenings — not the coal heat and the particular mustiness of the old wood floors, which he could have described with some precision by now, but something warmer laid over them. He set his briefcase against the wall and hung his coat on the hook and stood in the hallway.

Chicken. Something with chicken.

He had not made a note of any occasion.

Henry was in the sitting room with the newspaper folded across one knee. He looked up over the top of it.

"Evening."

"Evening," Marcus said. "You came back early."

"Three o'clock as usual." Henry turned a page. "You're late."

"The composition prompts," Marcus said. "Third period. I stayed to mark them."

"How'd they do."

"Better than November."

Henry received this and went back to the newspaper. The room settled. From the kitchen came the steady sound of Lillian doing something with water, and then the click of an oven handle, and then quiet. Marcus took the armchair on the near side and sat with his coat across his knees. The school had produced a composition from the second-year German class on the theme of eine Reise — a journey — and the results had been, as the results usually were, a demonstration of the gap between what a student knows in English and what they can render in German, the imagination outrunning the grammar, the subordinate clauses failing at the verb. He had marked them in the faculty room before gathering his things and was not, now that he was in this room with Henry's newspaper turning and the smell of whatever Lillian had in the oven, going to think about them further until morning.

The light in the sitting room came in at the west window from the last of the afternoon sun and fell across the floor in the way it fell in May and nowhere else — a quality of going-away that was not yet dark.

Henry turned another page.

---

They ate at half past five.

The chicken had come, Lillian said, from the Dunbar property. The neighbor three houses up had a laying hen that had stopped laying, and Mrs. Dunbar had preferred to make some use of it before summer than not; what had been given in return was not specified and Marcus did not ask. It was a good meal — chicken jointed and roasted with dried herbs from the pantry, potatoes, the first of the spring greens from the kitchen-garden bed under the south window. Marcus served himself and ate.

Henry mentioned the furnace.

"There was a memo," he said. "Second one. The first one said the budget was under review for April. This one says they reviewed it."

"And the determination?"

"The furnace is adequate."

"For whom?"

Henry considered. "For the principal's office, I would guess. The third-floor corridor's a different question. The third-floor corridor doesn't vote on budget determinations."

Marcus said he had expected the determination. Henry said it was the determination that had always been made in the history of the school's furnace and would continue to be made in the history of the school's furnace until the furnace failed at a moment that could not be deferred or reframed. He ate potato. Marcus said this was the administration of all things. Henry agreed it was. He poured water into his glass and set the pitcher down near the center of the table.

Lillian mentioned, not quite toward the end of the main course, that the Ladies' Auxiliary was doing another wool collection. Third one since November, which had required reclassifying the third as a spring drive, since the previous two had not met the quota and the wool needed was still needed. Socks, she said. Always socks. She mentioned this without particular emphasis, in the way she mentioned things at the table that were observable facts of the town's winter and were now observable facts of its spring. Marcus asked what the deadline was. She said the fourteenth of the month. He asked whether there was a drop point or a collection. She said the church vestibule, Saturdays, which she preferred because it meant she could do it after the marketing and not have to make a separate trip.

He asked something else, he thought — something appropriate, one of the questions that were appropriate when something had been mentioned and acknowledgment was expected without inquiry being intrusive. He ate. Henry ate. The radio in the next room was off; Henry had not turned it on this evening, which was not unusual for a Tuesday.

He was thinking, at a low level of his attention, about the composition on eine Reise. A student named Carroll had written, with some confidence, about a journey by train from Berlin to Vienna, which was geographically functional but which Marcus had been obliged to mark down for the second-person construction that Carroll had used as a way of avoiding the accusative throughout, and which had also contained a sentence that Marcus had read three times in the faculty room before identifying its error: the student had written *ich bin angekommen* and then, in the following clause, *ich bin gereist*, which was not wrong in itself but which had produced a tense sequence that implied the arrival had preceded the journey, the destination reached before the road was taken. Marcus had marked it and written *Zeitenfolge* in the margin and then, because *Zeitenfolge* assumed more knowledge of grammatical terminology than a second-year student was likely to have, had written *sequence of tenses — check* beside it in English.

In the gap between the main course and whatever Lillian was going to bring next, when the conversation had paused in the way it paused at this table without anything being wrong — Henry cutting carefully at the last of the chicken near the bone, the room quiet, the street outside the window gone from late-afternoon into the early grey of a May evening — Marcus said: "I think I may have known who the man on the breakwater was."

He did not look up.

He said: "From before. From another time."

Henry was quiet.

He set the knife down across the rim of the plate. He sat with his hands on the table for a moment, and then he put them in his lap, and he looked — not at Marcus, not at Lillian, but at some point of the room between the two, the wall above the sideboard — and he nodded. Once, slowly. Not agreement; not surprise. The nod of a man who has had the shape of a thing confirmed that he had been carrying as a supposition, without saying so, for some time.

The kitchen was silent. Then the sound of Lillian setting something down.

After a moment Henry said: "That happens in a war." A pause. "A man gets far from home and farther still, and then he runs out of road."

He picked up his fork.

He did not say: who was he? How do you know? Are you going to tell someone? Are you going to tell the harbormaster's office, or the county examiner's office, or the District Commander at Rockland? He did not ask what kind of before, or what kind of another time. He ate the last of the chicken. He reached for his water glass.

The kitchen door opened and Lillian came through with the water pitcher. She went to Marcus's glass first and poured. She went to Henry's and poured. She set the pitcher down on the sideboard and stood for a moment, and then she lifted the serving fork and cut more of the chicken onto Marcus's plate — the last of what was on the serving dish, which she had been keeping on the trivet — and set the serving fork down and sat.

She did not ask whether he wanted it.

She began to eat.

---

The subject did not come back. Marcus did not raise it. Henry did not raise it. Lillian did not indicate, in any way available to her, that there was anything at the table still requiring attention.

Henry asked, when Lillian had brought the stewed fruit and they were eating it, whether Marcus had gotten any further with the Carroll boy and the subordinate clause problem. Marcus said Carroll understood the constructions well enough in isolation; the difficulty was in extended writing, where the clause that was available and the clause that was correct could feel interchangeable at the rate Carroll worked. Henry said that sounded like a student worth the effort. Marcus said he thought so. Henry said his experience of students worth the effort was that they were worth the effort over a longer arc than any individual assignment suggested, and that the assignment was not the measure. Marcus said he had come to the same conclusion. They finished the fruit. Lillian cleared the stewed-fruit dishes.

After the meal Henry moved to the armchair with his newspaper. Lillian went to the kitchen counter and did something there — the sequence of sounds Marcus had charted precisely over twenty months: plates set to the side, the tap water run and shut, the particular sound of the dish rack being populated one plate at a time, and then the far cabinet, and then quiet. Marcus cleared the table. He had always cleared the table; it had been established in his first two weeks in the house and had not been discussed since. He brought the plates through to the kitchen doorway and Lillian took them, and he brought the water glasses and the serving things, and she took those too. He came back through to the dining room and pushed the chairs in.

The table was empty. The last light from the west window was nearly gone.

He said goodnight to Henry. Henry said goodnight without looking up from the newspaper. He said goodnight to Lillian through the kitchen doorway. She said goodnight and told him there was bread on the counter if he wanted it in the morning.

He went upstairs.

---

The room was dark. He lit the lamp on the desk and let it settle to its ordinary height.

The room was the room it had been this morning: the composition papers stacked in the right-hand corner, the pen in its groove beside the inkstand, the German grammar open to the subjunctive chapter on the reference shelf where he had left it before breakfast. The bottom drawer of the desk was closed.

He sat at the desk.

He had said: from before, from another time. He had not said Josef Lutz. He had not said Sherbrooke, or a road in October rain, or the name on a piece of water-damaged paper, or the name of the man in Montreal who had helped with certain practical details of a departure. He had not said these things because to say them would have required an account that no part of this evening had been arranged to receive — not Henry's newspaper, not the table, not the hour. The documents upstairs would have required explanation. Explaining them would have required explaining himself, in ways and to depths he had not been asked to go, in a house that had not asked him to go there.

He had said: I think I may have known. He had said: from another time. Henry had said: a man gets far from home and farther still, and then he runs out of road. None of what had been said at the table was imprecise. It was a partial account offered without terms and received without terms, which was the form the table could hold and which was, Marcus had to conclude, the form that had been required.

The bottom drawer was closed. He sat with his hands flat on the desk surface and listened to the sounds from below — Henry's newspaper settling, the last of Lillian's work in the kitchen, the house at its ordinary Tuesday-evening quiet. No radio tonight. A door somewhere closing.

He was not alone with it.

He had not been certain, until now, that this was a state of affairs that the situation allowed. Henry's nod had covered the question without answering it; Henry's sentence had covered it without requiring it to be asked. This was the skill of the man, perhaps, or the skill of a life in which the accurate reading of rooms had mattered practically, not academically — the reading done and the response made and the conversation continued, because continuation was what the room could hold.

The lamp made its circle on the desk.

After a few minutes he got up, undressed, and went to bed.

Below, the house went quiet by degrees, the way it went quiet on all the evenings when nothing required it to be otherwise.

input.summary: Tuesday evening, May 1944. Marcus walks home from school along Prospect Street, comes through the Crow gate, finds the house smelling of chicken (traded from the Dunbar neighbor's non-laying hen). The evening is the ordinary evening of the Crow house: Henry in the armchair with the newspaper, Lillian cooking, the table at half past five. The household conversation covers the principal's second furnace memo (determination: the furnace is adequate) and the Ladies' Auxiliary's third wool collection drive, reclassified as a spring drive. Marcus eats and participates in the way that has become natural over twenty months. In the gap between the main course and dessert — a gap that carries no more weight than any other — Marcus says, without looking up: "I think I may have known who the man on the breakwater was. From before. From another time." Henry is quiet. He sets his knife down. He nods once, slowly. After a moment he says: "That happens in a war. A man gets far from home and farther still, and then he runs out of road." He picks up his fork. Lillian comes from the kitchen, refills both water glasses, cuts the last of the chicken onto Marcus's plate without asking, sits. The subject does not return. The rest of the meal is ordinary — a discussion of the Carroll boy's subordinate-clause problem in German class, stewed fruit, Henry reading. Marcus clears the table as always. He goes upstairs. He sits at the desk. The bottom drawer is closed. He does not open it. He sits for a few minutes, listening to the house below, then gets up and goes to bed.

From before. From another time."* Henry nods once, slowly, and says: *"That happens in a war. A man gets far from home and farther still, and then he runs out of road."* He picks up his fork. input.content:
# Chapter 12 — Not Yet

The afternoon was hot in the way June could be before the fog came in from the south — a still, white heat that settled into the upstairs room and didn't move, the air through the open window no cooler than the air that had been in the room since noon. Hannah had pushed the window up as far as it would go. The upper pasture lay flat and white in the light, the haze low over the grass, and along the far fence four shapes moved slowly in a line following the hawthorn hedge. At this distance they were just men working. She had made a practice of not trying to tell them apart at this distance. The habit had cost her something in the winter and spring, and she was keeping it now.

Carvell Oakes was on the fence rail with his hat tipped forward. He had been there the same way for twenty minutes.

She was at her desk with the letter to her cousin Elsa, who lived with the Heger side of the family in Vermont and who wrote back in the careful English of someone who had learned it differently. Hannah had been at the letter since after the midday meal. She had covered the garden — the peas were doing well this year, the carrots still in the ground — and the weather, and the price Atwood's was asking for the sugar that had come through in May. She had said that the county fair might happen in August. She had said she hoped Elsa could come.

She was on her second page and had run, honestly, out of things she wanted to say. She wrote one more sentence about the peas, which was true, and re-read the letter from the beginning. It was the letter of a person who was alive and in Maine and thinking about her cousin in Vermont. That was all accurate. She folded the second page back and held it with her hands flat on the desk.

From below came the smell of the rhubarb Marta was putting up in the kitchen — the sharp, particular sweetness of cooked fruit and sugar, rising through the house.

---

Her father's step on the stairs was distinct. There was a creak on the fourth stair from the top that he hit the same way every time — in the middle, with his full weight — and she heard it before he was halfway up. She put the pen down. He appeared in the doorway without knocking.

"Hanna." The German form — the house form, the private one, the one without the English H at the end. He was already moving past her desk. "Der alte Stallmantel —" He switched without pausing, the way he did when his mind was on something practical. "The barn coat. I think I left my tobacco in the pocket."

"It's in the closet," she said.

He went past her to the closet and opened the door. She picked up her pen and held it over the letter without writing. Outside, through the window, the four shapes at the far fence had rounded the corner of the hawthorn hedge and were working south. She could hear the barn coat come off its hook and heard her father go through the pockets — the soft searching sound of hands finding nothing, the slight collapse of an empty pocket.

"Nichts," he said.

He moved again. She heard his boot settle on the closet floor.

She had moved the school bag to the closet in May, after re-sewing the lining with the note back inside. Before that it had hung on the hook by the stairs — she had put it there last December, when she'd wanted it somewhere she could get to easily, to know it was there. In May she had looked at the bag on the hook by the stairs and decided the closet was better. Her room. The closet inside her room. There was nothing to see in the bag even if you opened it; the note was in the lining, and the lining looked like lining. But she wanted the closet.

She did not hear him lift the bag or open it. She heard his boot shift on the floor, and then the step back.

"Danke, Hanna," her father said.

The German name, said without thinking — the name of the house, the name of the family, the language the note was written in. His footsteps went to the door. She heard the fourth stair on the way down, and then the third, and then the kitchen.

---

She set the pen on the desk.

She counted a full minute by the second hand of the clock on the shelf — the hand going all the way around once, ordinary time. The room was the same room. Through the window the far field was the same field.

She got up and went to the closet.

The barn coat was on its hook, the pockets flat. Below it: the school bag, its strap looped over the low hook she had added inside the closet door in May, the bag resting against the wall. She took it down and held it by the strap and pressed the bottom lightly. The stiffness was there — the faint, dense difference at the bottom inside seam where the note was, where the canvas didn't give quite the same as the rest. Seven stitches and a knot. Black thread, wrong-colored from the first.

She put the bag back. She closed the closet door.

The letter to Elsa was on the desk. She looked at it for a moment and then laid it face-down on the stack of papers beside the inkwell.

---

At four o'clock the crew came down off the slope and formed up near the wagon road for Oakes to walk them to the truck. Hannah was at the pump rinsing the milk pails. She watched without watching: Oakes moving along the line, the truck at the road's end idling, the men going up the step and disappearing into the back. Karl was third. He did not look toward the house.

She scoured the pails and hung them on the fence rail to drain. She went to the henhouse to check the water. The henhouse was hot, the air inside dense with the smell of birds and straw. She pulled the water dish and rinsed it at the spigot and brought it back. The hens moved aside. She latched the door and went back into the yard, the evening light going flat and golden across the fields now, the heat releasing slowly.

At supper Werner mentioned that the lower fence would need mending before the herd went back to the east pasture; he thought that would be by Thursday. He wanted her to pull wire on Saturday morning. Hannah said she would. Marta had saved some of the rhubarb for the table, in a dish, and Hannah ate it with her bread. Werner said the weather would hold for the weekend and then thought of something else and went quiet. They ate the rest of the meal without much said.

Werner went to bed early. He had been going early for several weeks now, coming off the day's work and going straight upstairs, not staying for the radio or the newspaper — just up, the stair creak, the footsteps above. He had been tired, or something that looked like tired; Hannah had not asked.

Marta took her mending to the sitting room. Hannah sat at the kitchen table for a few minutes, listening to the needle from the other room, and then she went upstairs.

---

The room still held the day's heat. She lit the oil lamp and let it steady, and then she carried the school bag from the closet to the bed and sat beside it.

The seam. She found the bottom inside corner and worked her fingertip along the black thread until the first stitch gave. She had done this enough times now that it opened for her, the stitches releasing in order, and she worked the note out slowly, one corner at a time, until it came free.

Four folds, the paper gone soft along the creases. She unfolded it on her knee.

Karl's side: pencil, small and upright, the kind of handwriting from schools where you copied things carefully and exactly. She did not read the first part. She knew it well enough to say it, and that wasn't what tonight was for. She went to the bottom: *Den Mann auf dem Weg habe ich noch in Erinnerung. Er schien einen langen Weg vor sich zu haben.*

She turned it.

Her own hand — smaller and more careful than her ordinary hand, pressed lighter, the way she'd written when she wanted the letters to take up as little room as possible. *Wilder's Landing, Küstenstraße. Oktober 1943 — Donnerstag oder Freitag, nachts, gegen zehn oder elf.* The account below that, in the order Karl had given it: the rain, the branch across the road, the truck slowing. Einen Mann zu Fuß. Älter. Schmächtig. Einen langen Mantel, nicht für das Wetter. Trug etwas, nah am Körper. Bewegte sich Richtung Wasser.

*Sah sich um. Lief weiter.*

---

She got up and carried the note to the lamp.

She held the left corner — Karl's corner, the penciled lines — and brought the paper toward the flame. She stopped when she could feel the heat on the backs of her fingers. An inch from the flame, maybe a little less.

The lamp burned without wavering. The evening had gone completely still; no air moved through the window. She held the note steady.

The yellowing began at the bottom margin. Not burning — just the paper changing from the heat, the way very old paper went at the edges over years in a warm room — except this was happening now, as she stood there. A thin strip of it, the color of old tea, moving upward from the corner where the warmth was closest. The paper stiffened slightly where it yellowed. The smell that came off it was not burning — not yet — just the smell of heat and pencil lead and old paper, something that had no other name, the smell of a thing that had been handled many times beginning to be something else.

She held it there.

Her fingers were warm. The note was warm. Werner upstairs, perhaps asleep. Marta's mending below. The far field dark now, the crew long gone from it, Karl somewhere she couldn't see and had no business thinking toward.

She could not have said how long she stood there. When she looked at the bottom margin again the yellow strip was a little wider than it had been.

She pulled the note back.

---

She took it to the bed. She unfolded it, pressed each fold flat, and folded it again along the same four creases. At the bottom left corner — Karl's corner — the paper had gone a darker yellow-brown, a strip the width of her thumbnail where the heat had been closest. Not a burn mark; it hadn't gotten that far. Just the color of the paper, changed.

She threaded the needle from Marta's sewing box and sewed the lining closed. Seven stitches, the knot she had learned to make so the thread didn't work loose from ordinary handling. Black thread. Wrong color, as always.

She bit the thread and put the needle back.

She carried the bag to the closet and hung it on the low hook and stood for a moment with her hand on the closet door. Then she closed it.

---

She blew out the lamp.

The room came back slowly — dark first, and then the grey-blue of the June evening, the sky outside the window still holding color above the woodlot, the upper pasture a dark shape below it. Past nine o'clock and not full dark. The air through the window was cooler than it had been all day.

The closed closet door. The window and the evening beyond it.

From the sitting room below: Marta's mending. The soft, regular click of the needle case, the thread pulling, the rhythm of work going on in a house that had gone otherwise quiet.

input.oneLine: Werner searches Hannah's room for tobacco and misses the note by inches; that evening Hannah holds it to the lamp flame, watches the margin yellow, and pulls it back — keeping it, now, by explicit choice.

input.summary: June 1944, humid afternoon. Hannah is in her room writing a letter to her cousin Elsa in Vermont — a real, ordinary letter. Below, Marta is putting up rhubarb preserves. The POW crew is in the far field; Carvell Oakes dozes on the fence rail. Werner comes upstairs looking for the tobacco he left in the barn coat — hung in Hannah's closet since last spring. He opens the closet, checks the coat pockets, finds nothing. His boot settles on the closet floor beside the school bag. He does not look at it. He says 'Danke, Hanna' — the German name, the house name — and goes back downstairs. Hannah sits at her desk for a full minute without moving. Then she goes to the closet, takes the bag down, presses the bottom to feel the note's stiffness through the lining, puts it back, and closes the door. She cannot return to the letter. The afternoon continues: crew leaves at four (Karl does not look toward the house), farm chores, ordinary supper (Werner mentions the lower fence, Marta's rhubarb on the table). Werner goes to bed early — he has been doing this for several weeks. After supper, Hannah goes upstairs, opens the lining, takes out the two-sided note, reads Karl's final sentences and then her own transcription on the reverse. She carries the note to the oil lamp. Holds the left corner near the flame — an inch away. The paper yellows along the bottom margin. She holds it there. She pulls it back. She folds it along the same four creases, threads the needle, re-sews the lining with seven stitches, and puts the bag back on the hook inside the closet door. She blows out the lamp. Literary-fade ending: the closed closet door, the June evening light through the window, Marta's mending from the sitting room below.
newFacts: Werner searched Hannah's room looking for tobacco in the barn coat (hung in Hannah's closet); he did not find the note — his boot settled on the closet floor near the school bag but he did not lift or open the bag.

Hannah moved the school bag from the hook by the stairs (where it had been since December 1943) to a low hook inside her bedroom closet door in May 1944 — a deliberate choice to keep it in her own room.

The note now carries a physical mark: a strip of yellow-brown discoloration at the bottom left corner (Karl's corner), the width of Hannah's thumbnail, from being held near the lamp flame. The paper is whole — it did not burn.
Hannah has explicitly chosen to keep the note. Before this chapter she kept it by not destroying it; now she has held it to the flame and pulled it back. The keeping is an active, named decision.
Werner Pfeiffer has been going to bed early for several weeks — since before the POW crew returned in March 1944. He does not explain this.
Marta Pfeiffer was putting up rhubarb preserves in the kitchen on this June afternoon; she brought some to the supper table.
